Three iterations of the PlayStation's [controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_controller "Game controller") were released over the console's lifespan. The first controller, the [PlayStation controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_controller "PlayStation controller"), was released alongside the PlayStation in December 1994. It features four individual directional buttons (as opposed to a conventional [D-pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-pad "D-pad")), a pair of [shoulder buttons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoulder_buttons "Shoulder buttons") on both sides, Start and Select buttons in the centre, and four face buttons consisting of simple geometric shapes: a green triangle, red circle, blue cross, and a pink square ([![Image 30: Triangle](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/PlayStationTriangle.svg/20px-PlayStationTriangle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PlayStationTriangle.svg "Triangle"), [![Image 31: Circle](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/PlayStationCircle.svg/20px-PlayStationCircle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PlayStationCircle.svg "Circle"), [![Image 32: Cross](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/PlayStationCross.svg/20px-PlayStationCross.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PlayStationCross.svg "Cross"), [![Image 33: Square](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/PlayStationSquare.svg/20px-PlayStationSquare.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PlayStationSquare.svg "Square")).[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-controllersquare-181) Rather than depicting traditionally used letters or numbers onto its buttons, the PlayStation controller established a trademark which would be incorporated heavily into the PlayStation brand. Teiyu Goto, the designer of the original PlayStation controller, said that the circle and cross represent "yes" and "no", respectively (though this layout is reversed in Western versions); the triangle symbolises a point of view and the square is equated to a sheet of paper to be used to access menus.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-1upcontroller-182)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonnell1995-160) The European and North American models of the original PlayStation controllers are roughly 10% larger than its Japanese variant, to account for the fact the average person in those regions has larger hands than the average Japanese person.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith199616-183)

Sony's first analogue gamepad, the [PlayStation Analog Joystick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Analog_Joystick "PlayStation Analog Joystick") (often erroneously referred to as the "Sony Flightstick"), was first released in Japan in April 1996. Featuring two parallel joysticks, it uses potentiometer technology previously used on consoles such as the [Vectrex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vectrex "Vectrex"); instead of relying on binary eight-way switches, the controller detects minute angular changes through the entire range of motion. The stick also features a thumb-operated digital hat switch on the right joystick, corresponding to the traditional D-pad, and used for instances when simple digital movements were necessary.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMao199624-184) The Analog Joystick sold poorly in Japan due to its high cost and cumbersome size.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams199720-185)

The increasing popularity of 3D games prompted Sony to add analogue sticks to its controller design to give users more freedom over their movements in virtual 3D environments.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-gaydarcontrollers-186) The first official analogue controller, the [Dual Analog Controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_Analog_Controller "Dual Analog Controller"), was revealed to the public in a small glass booth at the 1996 PlayStation Expo in Japan,[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams199720-185) and released in April 1997 to coincide with the Japanese releases of analogue-capable games _[Tobal 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobal\_2 "Tobal 2")_ and _[Bushido Blade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bushido\_Blade\_(video\_game) "Bushido Blade (video game)")_.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-187) In addition to the two analogue sticks (which also introduced two new buttons mapped to clicking in the analogue sticks), the Dual Analog controller features an "Analog" button and [LED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED "LED") beneath the "Start" and "Select" buttons which toggles analogue functionality on or off.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-gaydarcontrollers-186) The controller also features [rumble support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haptic_technology "Haptic technology"), though Sony decided that haptic feedback would be removed from all overseas iterations before the United States release.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-firsts-188) A Sony spokesman stated that the feature was removed for "manufacturing reasons", although rumours circulated that Nintendo had attempted to legally block the release of the controller outside Japan due to similarities with the [Nintendo 64 controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_64_controller "Nintendo 64 controller")'s [Rumble Pak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble_Pak "Rumble Pak"). However, a Nintendo spokesman denied that Nintendo took legal action. _[Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next\_Generation\_(magazine) "Next Generation (magazine)")_'s Chris Charla theorised that Sony dropped vibration feedback to keep the price of the controller down.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTECharla1997a26-189)

In November 1997, Sony introduced the [DualShock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DualShock "DualShock") controller. Its name derives from its use of two (dual) vibration motors (shock).[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-IGNcontrollers-190) Unlike its predecessor, its analogue sticks feature textured rubber grips, longer handles, slightly different shoulder buttons and has rumble feedback included as standard on all versions.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFerran201526-191) The DualShock later replaced its predecessors as the default controller.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-controllersquare-181)

### Functionality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=PlayStation_(console)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Functionality")]

In addition to playing games, most PlayStation models are equipped to play [CD-Audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CD-Audio "CD-Audio"). The Asian model SCPH-5903 can also play [Video CDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_CD "Video CD").[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWest199724-201) Like most CD players, the PlayStation can play songs in a programmed order, shuffle the playback order of the disc and repeat one song or the entire disc. Later PlayStation models use a [music visualisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_visualization "Music visualization") function called SoundScope. This function, as well as a memory card manager, is accessed by starting the console without either inserting a game or closing the CD tray, thereby accessing a [graphical user interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") (GUI) for the PlayStation BIOS.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-edgehistory-34) The GUI for the PS One and PlayStation differ depending on the firmware version: the original PlayStation GUI had a dark blue background with rainbow graffiti used as buttons, while the early PAL PlayStation and PS One GUI had a grey blocked background with two icons in the middle.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry199553-202)

PlayStation [emulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console_emulator "Video game console emulator") is versatile and can be run on numerous modern devices.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-203)[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-204)[Bleem!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleem! "Bleem!") was a commercial emulator which was released for [IBM-compatible PCs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") and the Dreamcast in 1999. It was notable for being aggressively marketed during the PlayStation's lifetime, and was the centre of multiple controversial lawsuits filed by Sony. Bleem! was programmed in [assembly language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language"), which allowed it to emulate PlayStation games with improved visual fidelity, enhanced resolutions, and filtered textures that was not possible on original hardware.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-bleem-205) Sony sued Bleem! two days after its release, citing [copyright infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement") and accusing the company of engaging in [unfair competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unfair_competition "Unfair competition") and [patent infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") by allowing use of PlayStation BIOSs on a Sega console.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-206) Bleem! were subsequently forced to shut down in November 2001.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-207)

### Copy protection system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=PlayStation_(console)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Copy protection system")]

Sony was aware that using CDs for game distribution could have left games vulnerable to [piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_piracy "Video game piracy"), due to the growing popularity of [CD-R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CD-R "CD-R") and [optical disc drives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_drive "Optical disc drive") with burning capability. To preclude illegal copying, a proprietary process for PlayStation [disc manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_Disc_manufacturing "Compact Disc manufacturing") was developed that, in conjunction with an augmented optical drive in Tiger H/E assembly, prevented burned copies of games from booting on an unmodified console. Specifically, all genuine PlayStation discs were printed with a small section of deliberate irregular data, which the PlayStation's optical pick-up was capable of detecting and [decoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency_modulation "Frequency modulation"). Consoles would not boot game discs without a specific wobble frequency contained in the data of the disc [pregap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregap "Pregap") sector (the same system was also used to encode discs' [regional lockouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_lockout "Regional lockout")).[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGreen2015255-208) This signal was within [Red Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Books "Rainbow Books") CD tolerances, so PlayStation discs' actual content could still be read by a conventional disc drive; however, the disc drive could not detect the wobble frequency (therefore duplicating the discs omitting it), since the laser pick-up system of any optical disc drive would interpret this wobble as an oscillation of the disc surface and compensate for it in the reading process.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki

The **Wii**[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-28) ([/w iː/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_WEE_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is a [home video game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_video_game_console "Home video game console") developed and marketed by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo"). It was released on November 19, 2006, in North America, and in December 2006 for most other regions of the world. It is Nintendo's fifth major home game console, following the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), and is a [seventh-generation console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Seventh generation of video game consoles") alongside [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft")'s [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360") and [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Interactive_Entertainment "Sony Interactive Entertainment")'s [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3").

The Nintendo president, [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata"), focused on appealing to a broader audience through innovative gameplay, rather than competing with Microsoft and Sony on raw computational power. [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto") and [Genyo Takeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genyo_Takeda "Genyo Takeda") led development, which was initially codenamed **Revolution**. The Wii emphasized new forms of interaction, particularly through its wireless controller, the [Wii Remote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote "Wii Remote"), which featured [motion-tracking controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_controller "Motion controller") and could [recognize gestures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gesture_recognition "Gesture recognition") and function as a [pointing device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointing_device "Pointing device"). The Wii was Nintendo's first console with native [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet") connectivity, enabling [online gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_game "Online game") and [digital distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") via the [Wii Shop Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Shop_Channel "Wii Shop Channel"). It also supported wireless connectivity with the handheld [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS") console for select games. Early models were backward-compatible with [GameCube games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_GameCube_games "List of GameCube games") and [accessories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_accessories "GameCube accessories"). Nintendo later released cheaper versions: the RVL-101, without GameCube compatibility, and the Wii Mini, which removed features such as online connectivity and [SD card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SD_card "SD card") storage.

Because of Nintendo's reduced focus on computational power, the Wii and [its games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Wii_games "List of Wii games") were less expensive to produce than those of its competitors. It was extremely popular at launch, and was in short supply in some markets. _[Wii Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Sports "Wii Sports")_, a [pack-in game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pack-in_game "Pack-in game"), became the Wii's [killer app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killer_application "Killer application") while new entries in the _[Super Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario "Super Mario")_, _[Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend\_of\_Zelda "Legend of Zelda")_, _[Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_(video\_game\_series) "Pokémon (video game series)")_, and _[Metroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metroid "Metroid")_ series helped boost its popularity. Within a year, the Wii became the best-selling console of the seventh generation and a social phenomenon in many countries. Total lifetime sales of the Wii reached over 101 million units. As of April 2026, it is the [seventh-best-selling console of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_game_consoles "List of best-selling game consoles"), and Nintendo's second best-selling home console after the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch") surpassed it in 2021.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Switch-30) The Wii was discontinued in October 2013, though the Wii Mini continued production for a few years, and some of its third party online services persisted until 2019.

The Wii repositioned Nintendo as a key player in the video game console marketplace, achieving Nintendo's goal of attracting a broader audience to video game consoles. The popularity of its motion-controlled games led Microsoft and Sony to develop the [Kinect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinect "Kinect") and [PlayStation Move](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Move "PlayStation Move"). However, the Wii's emphasis on casual-based experiences alienated core gamers. The Wii's successor, the [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U"), released in 2012, attempted to recapture that demographic but became a [commercial failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_failure "Commercial failure") and Nintendo's worst-selling home console.

## History

See also: [Seventh generation of video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Seventh generation of video game consoles")

### 2001–2003: Development

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Satoru_Iwata_-_Game_Developers_Conference_2011_-_Day_2_%283%29_%28cropped_2%29.jpg/250px-Satoru_Iwata_-_Game_Developers_Conference_2011_-_Day_2_%283%29_%28cropped_2%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Satoru_Iwata_-_Game_Developers_Conference_2011_-_Day_2_(3)_(cropped_2).jpg)

[Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo")'s president [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata") directed the company to design the Wii to appeal to a broader range of players.

Shortly after the release of the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), Nintendo began conceptual development on its next console.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-31) According to game designer [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto"), the company decided early to not aim to compete on hardware power, instead prioritizing new gameplay experiences.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:6-32)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-businessweek_big_ideas_pg1-33) The project was initially referred to by the placeholder name "GameCube Next" (GCNext or GCN).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:6-32)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-34) Nintendo originally envisioned pricing the console at around [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")100(equivalent to $182 in 2025).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:6-32)

On September 24, 2001, Nintendo began collaborating with Gyration Inc., a company that held several patents in [motion-sensing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_detector "Motion detector") technology, to prototype motion-based input devices using Gyration's patents.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-gizmodo_gyration-35)

After succeeding [Hiroshi Yamauchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshi_Yamauchi "Hiroshi Yamauchi") as Nintendo president in May 2002,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-36)[Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata") acknowledged that the company had fallen behind industry trends, particularly in online gaming. He also wanted Nintendo to develop hardware and video games that would appeal to all demographics.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-IGN_iwata_bio-37) Internal market research revealed that Nintendo's prior focus on unconventional hardware had made its platforms more difficult for third-party developers to support, weakening its competitive position.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInoue200927%E2%80%9331-38) One of Iwata's first major initiatives in response was the development of the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS"), a dual-screen handheld console with a [touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen "Touchscreen"), to revitalize their handheld console line.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-39)

In 2003, Iwata met with Miyamoto and [Genyo Takeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genyo_Takeda "Genyo Takeda") to discuss the company's market strategy. He directed Takeda to "go off the tech roadmap" in designing the new console, emphasizing that it needed to be accessible, especially to non-traditional audiences, including mothers.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInoue200937%E2%80%9338-40) He also wanted backward compatibility with earlier Nintendo games to reduce household clutter.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-businessweek_big_ideas_pg2-41) Takeda led hardware development, while Miyamoto focused on designing a new controller, leveraging Gyration's motion-sensing technology.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-gizmodo_gyration-35) Iwata proposed using motion controls as a means to simplify the gaming interface and expand its appeal.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-42) An initial prototype was completed within six months.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEInoue200943%E2%80%9345-43)

The Nintendo DS was said to have influenced the design of the new console. Nintendo observed that the DS's novel dual-screen interface had attracted non-traditional players and aimed to replicate that success on their home console platform.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-businessweek_big_ideas_pg2-41) Designer Ken'ichiro Ashida recalled, "We had the DS on our minds as we worked on the Wii. We thought about copying the DS's touch-panel interface and even came up with a prototype." The idea was ultimately abandoned to avoid redundancy between the two systems. Miyamoto later remarked, "If the DS had flopped, we might have taken the Wii back to the drawing board."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-businessweek_big_ideas_pg1-33)

### 2004–2005: Announcements

At [E3 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2004 "E3 2004"), Iwata first unveiled some details of the project under its new codename, "Revolution," a reflection of his belief the console would revolutionize the gaming industry.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-IGN_iwata_bio-37)[BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News "BBC News")' technology editor [Alfred Hermida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hermida "Alfred Hermida") wrote that Nintendo's struggle to match Sony and Microsoft in the home console market made success crucial.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-44)

The console, still named "Revolution", was formally presented to the public at [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3 "E3") in May 2005. At this time, the console's [motion controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_controller "Motion controller") was not yet finalized and was omitted from the unveiling.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-businessweek_big_ideas_pg1-33) Iwata held the console above him with one hand to emphasize its size relative to its rivals. The reduced form factor meant lower power consumption and less heat output,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesThiruvathukal201228-45) and was also designed to appeal to parents, who were thought to be more likely to allow the device into the living room if it was small and attractive.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesThiruvathukal2012102-46) The console's minimalist aesthetic invited comparisons to [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s original [iPod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPod "IPod").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesThiruvathukal201226%E2%80%9327-47) Iwata reportedly used a stack of three [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") cases as a reference for the final size.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesThiruvathukal201228-45) The prototype shown was black, though the final retail version, released the following year, was only available in white.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJonesThiruvathukal201226%E2%80%9327-47)

In September 2005, Iwata demonstrated a prototype of the controller at the [Tokyo Game Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Game_Show "Tokyo Game Show"). By this stage, the hardware closely resembled the final Wii Remote and [Nunchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunchuk_(controller) "Nunchuk (controller)"). During the presentation, Iwata demonstrated the controller's motion-sensing capabilities, supported a video with commentary from developers such as [Hideo Kojima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideo_Kojima "Hideo Kojima") and [Yuji Horii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuji_Horii "Yuji Horii"), who had tested the controller and believed people would be drawn in by it.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-48)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-49)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Wii_Peripherals_E3_2006_2.jpg/250px-Wii_Peripherals_E3_2006_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wii_Peripherals_E3_2006_2.jpg)

The Wii and several peripherals on display at E3 2006

The console's official name, "Wii," was announced in April, a month ahead of [E3 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2006 "E3 2006"). The stylized spelling—with two lowercase "i"s—was designed to represent both two people standing side by side and the pairing of the Wii Remote and Nunchuk.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-gamasutra_introducing_wii-50) In its announcement, Nintendo explained: "Wii sounds like 'we', which emphasizes that the console is for everyone. Wii can easily be remembered by people around the world, no matter what language they speak. No confusion."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-gamasutra_introducing_wii-50)

The name drew widespread mockery and criticism. _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ reported that Nintendo fans feared the name would perpetuate the perception that Nintendo made consoles primarily for children.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-51)_[BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC\_News "BBC News")_ reported the day after the name was announced that "a long list of puerile jokes, based on the name," had appeared on the Internet.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-52) Some [video game developers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") and journalists expressed a preference for the codename "Revolution."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-53) President of Nintendo of America [Reggie Fils-Aimé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Fils-Aim%C3%A9 "Reggie Fils-Aimé") defended the name, saying that the company chose the name over "Revolution" because they wanted something short, distinctive, and easily pronounceable in all cultures.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-54)

The Wii was made available for press demonstrations at E3 2006, where Nintendo also revealed several planned launch games. At the same event, the company reaffirmed its intention to release the console by the end of 2006.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-55)

### 2006–2010: Launch

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Wii_launch_in_Hamburg.jpg/250px-Wii_launch_in_Hamburg.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wii_launch_in_Hamburg.jpg)

Crowds gather in Hamburg to buy a Wii on launch day.

Nintendo announced the launch plans and pricing for the Wii in September 2006. The console first launched in the United States on November 19, 2006, priced at US$249.99(equivalent to $399.25 in 2025).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-NArelease-9) Other regional release dates and prices included Japan on December 2, priced at ¥25,000(equivalent to ¥28,401 in 2024),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-JPrelease-11) followed by Australasia on December 7 at A$399.95(equivalent to $592.54 in 2022),[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-AUSrelease-56) and later, the United Kingdom on December 8 for £179.99(equivalent to £311.06 in 2025), with most of Europe receiving it at €249.99.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-EUrelease-10) Nintendo aimed to have around 30 Wii games available by the end of 2006 and anticipated shipping over 4 million consoles by the year's end.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-cnn_launch_date-57)

As part of its launch campaign, Nintendo promoted the Wii in North America through a series of [television advertisements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_advertisement "Television advertisement") directed by Academy Award winner [Stephen Gaghan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Gaghan "Stephen Gaghan"). The internet ads campaign featured slogans like "Wii would like to play" and "Experience a new way to play". Launched in November 2006, the campaign had a budget exceeding $200 million for the year.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-58)

These ads targeted a broader demographic compared to other consoles, inviting parents and grandparents to experience the Wii.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-59) Nintendo's goal was to appeal to a wider audience than its competitors in the seventh generation.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-60) In December 2006, Iwata stated that Nintendo didn't view itself as "fighting Sony," but instead focused on how to expand the gaming demographic.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-61) This strategy proved successful as the Wii became a global social phenomenon throughout 2007.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-62)

The Wii's launch in other regions took several years. It arrived in South Africa on September 30, 2007,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-iol-2) South Korea on April 26, 2008,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-63) Taiwan on July 12, 2008,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-64) and Hong Kong on December 12, 2009.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-65). In India, it was distributed from September 30, 2008 through partnership between Samurai Electronics and HCL Infosystems.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-rediff-3)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-66) Nintendo had planned to work with its localization partner, [iQue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue "IQue"), to release the Wii in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") in 2008, but was unable to meet the requirements to circumvent the [ban on foreign-made consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_games_in_China#Chinese_console_ban_(2000%E2%80%932015) "Video games in China") imposed by the Chinese government.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-67)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-68)

### 2011–2014: Successor and discontinuation

Further information: [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Wii_U_Console_and_Gamepad.png/250px-Wii_U_Console_and_Gamepad.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wii_U_Console_and_Gamepad.png)

The Wii U, with its [Wii U GamePad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U_GamePad "Wii U GamePad") in front

Nintendo announced the successor to the Wii, the Wii U, at [E3 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2011 "E3 2011").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-69)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-70) Nintendo had recognized that the Wii had generally been shunned by the core gaming audience as it was perceived more as a casual gaming experience. The Wii U was aimed to draw the core audience back in with more advanced features atop the basic Wii technology.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-71)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-72) The Wii U features the [Wii U GamePad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U_GamePad "Wii U GamePad"), a controller with an embedded touchscreen, alongside output [1080p](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1080p "1080p")[high-definition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-definition_video "High-definition video") graphics. The Wii U GamePad serves as a secondary screen alongside the television. The Wii U is fully backward-compatible with Wii games and peripherals for the Wii, including the Wii Remote, Nunchuk controller and Wii Balance Board, and select Wii U games including support for these devices.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-73) The Wii U was first released on November 18, 2012 in North America; November 30, 2012 in Europe and Australia, and December 8, 2012 in Japan.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-74)

Nintendo continued to sell the revised Wii model and the Wii Mini alongside the Wii U during the Wii U's first release year. During 2013, Nintendo began to sunset certain Wii online functions as they pushed consumers towards the Wii U as a replacement system or towards the offline Wii Mini, though the Wii Shop Channel remained available.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-75) Nintendo discontinued production of the Wii in October 2013 after selling over 100 million units worldwide,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-76) though the company continued to produce the Wii Mini unit primarily for the North American market.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-77) The WiiConnect24 service and several channels based on that service were shuttered in June 2013.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-polygon_wiiconnect24_shutdown-22) Support for online multiplayer games via the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection were discontinued in May 2014,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-verge_wificonnection_shutdown-20) while the Wii Shop was closed in January 2019, effectively ending its online services.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-engadget_wiishop_closed-24)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-78) The Wii Mini continued to be manufactured for some time after.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-79)

Despite the Wii's discontinuation, some developers continued to produce Wii games. Ubisoft released _[Just Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just\_Dance\_(video\_game\_series) "Just Dance (video game series)")_ games for the Wii up to _[Just Dance 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just\_Dance\_2020 "Just Dance 2020")_ (2019).[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-80) Vblank Entertainment's _[Shakedown: Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakedown:\_Hawaii "Shakedown: Hawaii")_ along with _[Retro City Rampage DX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retro\_City\_Rampage\_DX "Retro City Rampage DX")_ are the most recent Wii games, which were released on July 9, 2020, more than 13 years after the Wii's launch.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-81)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-82) On January 27, 2020, Nintendo announced that from February 6 it will no longer repair Wii consoles due to a scarcity of spare parts.[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-84)

## Hardware

### Console

[![Image 12: Stack of video-game consoles, of which the Wii is the smallest](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/NintendoStack.jpg/250px-NintendoStack.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NintendoStack.jpg)

The Wii (top) compared in size to the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), [Nintendo 64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_64 "Nintendo 64"), North American [Super NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System"), and [NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Nintendo Entertainment System")

Nintendo chose not to outpace the performance of rival consoles. Unlike their previous consoles, they built the Wii from [commercial off-the-shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_off-the-shelf "Commercial off-the-shelf") hardware rather than developing customized components. This significantly reduced manufacturing costs, allowing Nintendo to offer the console at a lower price.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-fortune_2007-85) As Miyamoto explained, "Originally, I wanted a machine that would cost $100. My idea was to spend nothing on the console technology so all the money could be spent on improving the interface and software."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-86)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Nintendo-IBM-BROADWAY-1.webp/250px-Nintendo-IBM-BROADWAY-1.webp?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo-IBM-BROADWAY-1.webp)

[Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(microprocessor) "Broadway (microprocessor)") CPU

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Nintendo-HOLLYWOOD-1.webp/120px-Nintendo-HOLLYWOOD-1.webp?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo-HOLLYWOOD-1.webp)

[Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_(graphics_chip) "Hollywood (graphics chip)") SoC

The Wii's [central processing unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CPU "CPU"), named [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(microprocessor) "Broadway (microprocessor)"), is a [32-bit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32-bit_computing "32-bit computing") chip developed by [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"). Based on the same [PowerPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PowerPC "PowerPC") architecture as the GameCube's [Gekko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gekko_(processor) "Gekko (processor)") processor, it runs at 729 MHz and was manufactured using a more efficient [90 nm process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90_nm_process "90 nm process"), reducing power consumption by about 20% compared to Gekko's [180 nm process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180_nm_process "180 nm process").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-IGNTech-87)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Wii:_The_Total_Story-88)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-89) Other system functions are handled by [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_(graphics_chip) "Hollywood (graphics chip)"), a [system-on-a-chip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_on_a_chip "System on a chip") (SoC) developed by [ATI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATI_Technologies "ATI Technologies") that combines graphics, audio, and [input/output](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Input/output "Input/output") functions.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-IGNTech-87) Its [graphics processing unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit") (GPU) is an updated version of the GameCube's [Flipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATI_Flipper "ATI Flipper"), running at 243 MHz, 1.5 times faster, allowing it to support more advanced visual effects and including 3 MB of embedded texture memory. It also contains [Starlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_(graphics_chip)#Starlet "Hollywood (graphics chip)"), an [ARM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_architecture_family "ARM architecture family")-based coprocessor with 96 KB of RAM that manages input/output operations and system security. Hollywood integrates 24 MB of high-speed [1T-SRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1T-SRAM "1T-SRAM") that works alongside 64 MB of [GDDR3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDDR3_SDRAM "GDDR3 SDRAM") memory mounted on the motherboard, bringing the total system memory to 88 MB.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-IGNTech-87) In terms of computational power, the Wii was about 1.5 to 2 times more powerful than the GameCube,[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Wii:_The_Total_Story-88)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-ign_wii_faq-90) but was the least powerful of the major home consoles of its generation.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-91)

The Wii's motherboard has a [WiFi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WiFi "WiFi") module, supporting [802.11b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/802.11b "802.11b") and [802.11g](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/802.11g "802.11g") modes, and a [Bluetooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluetooth "Bluetooth") module to communicate with its controllers. A USB-based [LAN adapter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_interface_controller "Network interface controller") can connect the Wii to a wired Ethernet network.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-ign_wii_faq-90)

Games are read via a front slot-loading optical drive compatible with Nintendo's proprietary 12 cm [Wii discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_optical_discs "Nintendo optical discs") and 8 cm [GameCube discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_GameCube_Game_Disc "Nintendo GameCube Game Disc"). However, it does not support standard optical media such as DVDs or CDs. Although Nintendo had planned on incorporating this feature into later revisions of the Wii, the demand for the console meant a delay in their schedule, until the feature lost interest.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-92)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-93)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-94) Nintendo later explained that they felt that most consumers owned other devices with DVD playback capability, and it allowed them to avoid the additional cost associated with licensing patents for the technology.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-2011_E3_Expo_Analyst_Q_&_A_Session-95) The optical drive slot is illuminated with LEDs that indicate system activity, for example, pulsing blue when receiving messages via WiiConnect24 or during disc reading.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-96)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-97)

The system includes 512 MB of internal [flash memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_memory "Flash memory") for storing saved data and downloaded content. This storage could be expanded via [SD cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SD_card "SD card") inserted into a slot behind a front panel. A later system update enabled users to launch Wii channels and play [Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console") and [WiiWare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WiiWare "WiiWare") games directly from SD cards.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-98)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-99)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-100)

The rear of the console houses video output and power connectors, along with two [USB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USB "USB") ports. When oriented vertically, the top panel reveals four GameCube controller ports and two GameCube memory card slots.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Wii:_The_Total_Story-88)

At launch, the Wii was Nintendo's smallest home console. Measuring 44 [millimeters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millimetre "Millimetre") (1.73 [inches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inch "Inch")) wide, 157 mm (6.18 in) tall, and 215.4 mm (8.48 in) deep in its vertical orientation, the system was slightly larger than three [DVD cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_case "Keep case") stacked together. The console was designed to operate either horizontally or vertically.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_closer_look-101) Its included stand, used for stability in vertical placement, measures 55.4 mm (2.18 in) wide, 44 mm (1.73 in) tall, and 225.6 mm (8.88 in) deep. Weighing 1.2 [kilograms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram") (2.65 [pounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_(mass) "Pound (mass)")),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_closer_look-101) the Wii was the lightest of the three major seventh-generation consoles.

### Wii Remote

Main article: [Wii Remote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote "Wii Remote")

[![Image 15: Two types of Wii controllers, one in each hand](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Wiimote-in-Hands.jpg/250px-Wiimote-in-Hands.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiimote-in-Hands.jpg)

A [Nunchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Nunchuk "Wii Nunchuk"), Wii Remote and [strap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote#Strap "Wii Remote")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Wii_Demonstration_E3_2006.jpg/250px-Wii_Demonstration_E3_2006.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wii_Demonstration_E3_2006.jpg)

The Wii Remote being used to play _Metroid Prime 3_ at E3 2006. The Sensor Bar can be seen at the base of the television screen.

The Wii Remote[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-103) is the primary [controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_controller "Game controller") for the console. The remote contains a [MEMS-based](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microelectromechanical_systems "Microelectromechanical systems") three-dimension [accelerometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerometer "Accelerometer"), along with [infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared "Infrared") detection sensors located at the far end of the controller.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-nytimes_wii_remote-104)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-mit_review-105) The accelerometers allow the Wii Remote to recognize its orientation after being moved from a resting position, translating that motion into [gesture recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gesture_recognition "Gesture recognition") for a game.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-nytimes_wii_remote-104) For example, the pack-in game _Wii Sports_ includes a [ten-pin bowling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten-pin_bowling "Ten-pin bowling") game that has the player hold the Wii Remote and deliver a ball; the Wii Remote can account for the player's position relative to the Sensor Bar, and their arm and wrist rotation to apply speed and spin to the virtual ball's delivery on screen.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-106) The infrared detectors are used to track emissions from [LEDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-emitting_diode "Light-emitting diode") in the included [Sensor Bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensor_Bar "Sensor Bar"), which is placed above or below the television display, as to track the relative orientation of the Wii Remote towards the screen. This allows the Wii Remote to act as a [pointing device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointing_device "Pointing device") like a [computer mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_mouse "Computer mouse") on the television screen, with an approximate range of 15 feet (4.6 m) for accurate detection.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-nytimes_wii_remote-104)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_wii_review-107)

The Wii Remote features traditional controller inputs, including a [directional pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directional_pad "Directional pad"), three face action buttons, a shoulder trigger, and four system-related buttons including a power switch. The Wii Remote connects to the Wii via Bluetooth with an approximate 30 feet (9.1 m) range,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_wii_review-107) communicating the sensor and control information to the console unit. The Wii Remote includes an internal speaker and a [rumble pack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haptic_technology#Video_games "Haptic technology") that can be triggered by a game to provide feedback directly to the player's hand.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-nytimes_wii_remote-104) Up to four Wii Remotes could connect wirelessly to a Wii, with LED lights on each remote indicating which controller number the Remote had connected as.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_wii_review-107) The remote is [battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_battery "Electric battery")-operated, and when the Remote is not powered on, these LED lights can display the remaining battery power.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-nytimes_wii_remote_secrets-102)

A wrist-mounted strap is included with the Wii Remote, with one end affixed to the bottom of the unit. Nintendo strongly encouraged players to use the strap in case the Wii Remote accidentally slipped out of their hands. Nintendo recalled the original straps in December 2006 and provided a free, stronger strap as a replacement, as well as packaging the new strap in future bundles after the company faced [legal challenges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote#Legal_issues "Wii Remote") from users that reported damage to their homes from the Wii Remote slipping from their hands while playing.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-bbc_remote_breakages-108)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-109) In October 2007, Nintendo also added a [silicone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicone "Silicone")[Wii Remote Jacket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote_Jacket "Wii Remote Jacket") to shipments of the Wii and Wii Remote, as well as a free offering for existing users. The Jacket wraps around the bulk of the remote but leaves access to the various buttons and connectors, providing a stickier surface in the user's grip to further reduce the chance of the Remote falling out of the player's hand.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-110)

Accessories can be connected to a Wii Remote through a [proprietary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proprietary_hardware "Proprietary hardware") port at the base of the controller.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_wii_review-107) The Wii shipped with the bundled [Nunchuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Nunchuk "Wii Nunchuk")—a handheld unit with an accelerometer, [analog stick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_stick "Analog stick"), and two trigger buttons—which connected to this port on the Wii Remote via a cable 4 feet (1.2 m) in length. Players hold both the Wii Remote and Nunchuk in separate hands to control supported games.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-mit_review-105)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-111)

The [Wii MotionPlus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_MotionPlus "Wii MotionPlus") accessory plugs into the port at the base of the Wii Remote and augments the existing sensors with [gyroscopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyroscope "Gyroscope") to allow for finer motion detection.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-nytimes_wii_remote_secrets-102) The MotionPlus accessory was released in June 2009 with a number of new games directly supporting this new functionality, including _[Wii Sports Resort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Sports\_Resort "Wii Sports Resort")_ which included the accessory as part of a bundle.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-112) The MotionPlus functionality was later incorporated into a revision of the controller called the [Wii Remote Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Remote_Plus "Wii Remote Plus"), first released in October 2010.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-113)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-114)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-115) A number of third-party controller manufacturers developed their own lower-cost versions of the Wii Remote, though these generally were less accurate or lacked the sensitivity that Nintendo's unit had.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-116)

### Other controllers and accessories

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Wii-classic-controller.jpg/250px-Wii-classic-controller.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wii-classic-controller.jpg)

The original [Classic Controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Controller "Classic Controller") connected to the Wii Remote

The [Classic Controller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Controller "Classic Controller") is an extension for the Wii Remote, released alongside the Wii in November 2006. Its form factor is similar to classic gamepads such as that for the [Super Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System"), with a d-pad, four face buttons, Start and Select buttons alongside the Wii connection button, and two shoulder buttons. Additionally, Nintendo included inputs present in modern controllers, like 2 analog sticks and pressure sensitive shoulder buttons. Players can use it with older games from the Virtual Console in addition to games designed for the Wii.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-ZD_Classic-117) In 2009, Nintendo released the Wii Classic Controller Pro, which was modelled after the GameCube and PlayStation 2 controllers form factor and amongst other additions, adds grips on the bottom of the controller and rearranges the placement of the shoulder buttons. However, unlike the GameCube and original Classic Controller, the Classic Controller Pro does not have pressure sensitive shoulder buttons.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-118)

The [Wii Balance Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Balance_Board "Wii Balance Board") was released alongside _[Wii Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Fit "Wii Fit")_ in December 2007. It is a wireless [balance board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_board "Balance board") accessory for the Wii, with multiple pressure sensors used to measure the user's [center of balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_mass "Center of mass").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-119)_Wii Fit_ offers a number of different exercise modes which monitored the player's position on the board, as well as exercise gamification, as to encourage players to exercise daily.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-120) In addition to use in Nintendo's _[Wii Fit Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Fit\_Plus "Wii Fit Plus")_ that expanded the range of exercises using the Wii Balance Board, the accessory can be used in other third-party games that translated the player's balance on the unit into in-game controls such as _[Shaun White Snowboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun\_White\_Snowboarding "Shaun White Snowboarding")_ and _[Skate It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skate\_It "Skate It")_.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-121)[Namco Bandai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namco_Bandai_Games "Namco Bandai Games") produced a mat controller (a simpler, less-sophisticated competitor to the Balance Board).[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-122)

One of Iwata's initiatives at Nintendo was focused on "quality of life" products, those that encouraged players to do other activities beyond simply sitting and playing video games as to promote physical wellbeing. The use of motion controls in the Wii served part of this, but Nintendo developed additional accessories to give awareness of one's health as a lead-in for the company to break into the healthcare field.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-123) At [E3 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2009 "E3 2009"), Nintendo had presented a "[Vitality Sensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_rate_monitor "Heart rate monitor")" accessory that would be used to measure a player's pulse as a lead-in to a larger quality of life initiative, but this product was never released. In a 2013 Q&A, Satoru Iwata revealed that the Vitality Sensor had been shelved, as internal testing found that the device did not work with all users, and its use cases were too narrow.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-124) Despite this, Nintendo has continued Iwata's quality of life program with further products on later consoles and games.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-125)

A number of first- and third-party accessories were developed that the Wii Remote could be slotted into and then used in a more physical manner that took advantage of the accelerometer and gyroscopic functions of the controller. Some copies of _[Mario Kart Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_Wii "Mario Kart Wii")_ shipped with the [Wii Wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Wheel "Wii Wheel"), a plastic steering wheel frame with the Wii Remote could be inserted into, so that players could steer more effectively in game.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-126)[Rhythm games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_game "Rhythm game") that used plastic instruments, such as _[Guitar Hero III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero\_III "Guitar Hero III")_, shipped with instruments that the Wii Remote could be slotted into; the remote powered the various buttons on the controller and relayed that to the Wii.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-127)

### Variants and bundles

The Wii launch bundle included the console; a stand to allow the console to be placed vertically; a plastic stabilizer for the main stand, one Wii Remote, a Nunchuk attachment for the Remote, a Sensor Bar and a removable stand for the bar to mount on a television set, an external [power adapter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_supply "Power supply"), and two [AA batteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AA_battery "AA battery") for the Wii Remote. The bundle included a [composite A/V cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_video "Composite video") with [RCA connectors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_connector "RCA connector"), and in appropriate regions such as in Europe, a [SCART](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCART "SCART") adapter was also included.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-128) A copy of the game _[Wii Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Sports "Wii Sports")_ was included in most regional bundles.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-129)

Although Nintendo showed the console and the Wii Remote in white, black, silver, lime-green and red before it was released,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-130) it was only available in white for its first two-and-a-half years of sales. Black consoles were available in Japan in August 2009,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-131) in Europe in November 2009[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-132) and in North America in May 2010.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-133) A red Wii system bundle was available in Japan on November 11, 2010, commemorating the 25th anniversary of _[Super Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Bros. "Super Mario Bros.")_[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:0-134) The European version of the limited-edition red Wii bundle was released on October 29, 2010, which includes the original _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_(arcade\_game) "Donkey Kong (arcade game)")_ game pre-installed onto the console, _[New Super Mario Bros. Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Super\_Mario\_Bros.\_Wii "New Super Mario Bros. Wii")_ and _Wii Sports_.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:1-135) The red Wii bundle was released in North America on November 7, 2010, with _New Super Mario Bros. Wii_ and _Wii Sports_.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:2-136)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:3-137) All of the red Wii system bundles feature the Wii Remote Plus, with integrated Wii MotionPlus technology.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:0-134)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:1-135)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:2-136)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:3-137)

The prefix for the numbering scheme of the Wii system and its parts and accessories is "RVL-" for its [codename](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_name "Code name"), "Revolution". #### Cost-reduced model

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/WiiFamilyEdition.svg/250px-WiiFamilyEdition.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WiiFamilyEdition.svg)

RVL-101 layout with its labels aligned horizontally, just as it was designed to be placed, unlike the original model

A cost-reduced variant of the Wii (model RVL-101) was released late into the platform's lifespan that removed the GameCube controller ports and memory card slots found on the original model. This means that this model is incompatible with GameCube games alongside the GameCube Controller for Wii games that support it. This model is often referred to as the "Wii Family Edition", the name given to the bundle when it was first sold in Europe. Additionally, it does not include a stand, as it is intended to be positioned horizontally. Nintendo announced the new revision in August 2011 as a replacement for the original Wii model which it was discontinuing in certain regions including Europe and the United States.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-eurogamer_current_wii_discontinued-15)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:4-139) The new unit in its bundles was priced at $149.99,[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_redesign_release-140) a further reduction for the Wii's MSRP at the time of $199.99 established in September 2009.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-cnn_2009_price_drop-141)

The console was first released in North America on October 23, 2011, in a black finish, bundled with a black Wii Remote Plus and Nunchuk, along with _New Super Mario Bros. Wii_ and a limited-edition soundtrack for _[Super Mario Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Galaxy "Super Mario Galaxy")_.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_redesign_release-140) It was released in Europe on November 4, 2011, in a white finish, bundled with a white Wii Remote Plus and Nunchuk, along with _[Wii Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Party "Wii Party")_ and _Wii Sports_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Eurogamer_Wii_Family_Release-5) A special bundle featuring a blue version of the revised Wii model and Wii Remote Plus and Nunchuk with the inclusion of _[Mario & Sonic at the London 2012 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_&\_Sonic\_at\_the\_London\_2012\_Olympic\_Games "Mario & Sonic at the London 2012 Olympic Games")_ was released in Europe on November 18, 2011, in collaboration with [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-142) Nintendo later revised the North American bundle by replacing the prior pack-in game and soundtrack with the original _Wii Sports_ duology; the new bundle was released on October 28, 2012.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-143)

#### Wii Mini

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Wii-Mini-Console-Set-H.jpg/250px-Wii-Mini-Console-Set-H.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wii-Mini-Console-Set-H.jpg)

A Wii Mini with Wii Remote

The **Wii Mini** (model RVL-201)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-:4-139) is a smaller, redesigned Wii with a top-loading disc drive. In addition to the lack of GameCube support, the Wii Mini removes Wi-Fi support and online connectivity, along with the removal of the SD card slot. It also removed support for 480p and component video output.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-EurogamerWiiMiniReview-16) According to Nintendo of Canada's Matt Ryan, they stripped these features to bring down the price of the console further as to make it an option for those consumers that had not yet gotten a Wii or for those who wanted a second Wii in a different location. Ryan stated that while removing the online functionality would prevent some games from being played, most Wii games could still be played without it.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-polygon_wii_mini-144) The Wii Mini is styled in matte black with a red border, and includes a red Wii Remote Plus and Nunchuk. According to Ryan, the red coloring was indicative of the planned exclusive release in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-polygon_wii_mini-144) A composite A/V cable, wired Sensor Bar and power adapter are also included.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-engadget_wii_mini_review-145)

The Wii Mini was first released on December 7, 2012, exclusively in Canada with a MSRP of CA$99.99.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-engadget_wiimini_canada-6) It was later released in Europe on March 22, 2013,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-web.archive.org-7) and in the United States on November 17, 2013.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-polygon_wiimini_us-8) The Canadian and European releases did not include a game,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-engadget_wii_mini_review-145)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-146) while _Mario Kart Wii_ had been included in all launch bundles in the United States.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-polygon_wiimini_us-8) Nintendo added several best-selling and critically acclaimed Wii games to its [Nintendo Selects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Selects "Nintendo Selects") label and marketed those alongside the Wii Mini's release.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-engadget_wiimini_canada-6)

## Software

See also: [Wii system software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_system_software "Wii system software")

The console has many internal features made available from its hardware and [firmware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firmware "Firmware") components. The hardware allows for extendability (via expansion ports), while the firmware (and some software) could receive periodic updates via the [WiiConnect24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WiiConnect24 "WiiConnect24") service.

### Wii Menu

Main article: [Wii Menu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Menu "Wii Menu")

[![Image 20: Screenshot of Wii Menu](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/da/Wiimen.png/250px-Wiimen.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiimen.png)

Wii Menu

The development of the Wii Menu, the main user interface for the Wii, was led by Takashi Aoyama of Nintendo's Integrated Research & Development Division. The project, named the "Console Feature Realization Project", was to figure out what the Wii interface could show running in a low-power mode on an around-the-clock schedule that would be of interest for people to look at if they were not playing games.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_menu-147) The idea of having continually updated weather and news reports made logical sense from testing, and this led to the idea of presenting these similar to a row of televisions each set to a different [television channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_channel "Television channel") as if in an electronics shop, creating the "channels" concept. A user can navigate to any channel window to bring that to the forefront, whether to launch the game or application or to get more information that was being displayed.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_menu-147) For example, the Forecast Channel would display a brief summary of the local area's temperature and short-term weather forecast, while clicking on the channel brought up an interactive globe that the user could manipulate with the Wii Remote to explore real-time weather conditions across the Earth.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-148)

The Wii launched with six channels: the Disc Channel which was used to launch Wii and [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") games from an optical disc; the [Mii Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mii_Channel "Mii Channel") to create Mii avatars; the Photo Channel which could be used to view and edit photos stored on an SD card; the [Wii Shop Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Shop_Channel "Wii Shop Channel") to purchase new games and applications; the Forecast Channel and the News Channel.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_closer_look-101) In addition to default channels that came with the Wii, new channels could be added through system updates, downloaded applications from the Wii Shop Channel, or added by games themselves.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_menu-147) Shortly after launch, other free channels created by Nintendo were made available to users, including the [Internet Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Channel "Internet Channel"), a modified version of the [Opera web browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_(web_browser) "Opera (web browser)") for the Wii which supports [USB keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USB_keyboard "USB keyboard") input and [Adobe Flash Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adobe_Flash_Player "Adobe Flash Player").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_closer_look-101)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-149)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-150)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-151)

The Wii Menu channels feature music composed by video game composer [Kazumi Totaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazumi_Totaka "Kazumi Totaka").[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Skrebels_2021-152)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Brodeur_2020-153)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Robinson_2019-154)

The Wii introduced the use of player-customized avatars called Miis, which have been continued to be used by Nintendo in the Wii U, the Nintendo 3DS family, and, to a lesser extent, the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch"). Each player on a Wii console was encouraged to create their own Mii via the [Mii Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mii_Channel "Mii Channel") to be used in games like _[Wii Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Sports "Wii Sports")_ and some of the system software like the Mii Channel. For example, players would select their Mii in _Wii Sports_, creating their in-game avatar for the game. Miis could be shared with other players through the Mii Channel.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-pcworld_closer_look-101)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-155)

### Nintendo DS connectivity

The Wii system supports wireless connectivity with the Nintendo DS without any additional accessories. This connectivity allows the player to use the Nintendo DS microphone and touchscreen as inputs for Wii games. The first game utilizing Nintendo DS-Wii connectivity is _[Pokémon Battle Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Battle\_Revolution "Pokémon Battle Revolution")_. Players with either the [_Pokémon Diamond_ or _Pearl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Diamond_and_Pearl "Pokémon Diamond and Pearl") Nintendo DS games are able to play battles using the Nintendo DS as a controller.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-connectivity_returns-156)_[Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles: Echoes of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy\_Crystal\_Chronicles:\_Echoes\_of\_Time "Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles: Echoes of Time")_, released on both Nintendo DS and Wii, features connectivity in which both games can advance simultaneously. Nintendo later released the Nintendo Channel, which allows Wii owners to download [game demos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_demo "Game demo") of popular games such as _[Mario Kart DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_DS "Mario Kart DS")_, or additional data to their Nintendo DS in a process similar to that of a [DS Download Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DS_Download_Station "DS Download Station").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_menu-147)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-157) The console is also able to expand Nintendo DS games.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-connectivity_returns-156)

### Online connectivity

Main articles: [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection"), [WiiConnect24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WiiConnect24 "WiiConnect24"), [Internet Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Channel "Internet Channel"), [List of Wii Wi-Fi Connection games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Wii_Wi-Fi_Connection_games "List of Wii Wi-Fi Connection games"), and [Wii Menu §Downloadable channels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Menu#Downloadable_channels "Wii Menu")

The Wii console connects to the Internet through its built-in [802.11b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_802.11#802.11b "IEEE 802.11")/[g](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_802.11#802.11g "IEEE 802.11") Wi-Fi or through a USB-to-Ethernet adapter; either method allows players to access the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-Wii:_The_Total_Story-88) The service had several features for the console, including Virtual Console, WiiConnect24, the Internet Channel, the [Forecast Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forecast_Channel "Forecast Channel"), the [Everybody Votes Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everybody_Votes_Channel "Everybody Votes Channel"), the [News Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_Channel_(Wii) "News Channel (Wii)") and the [Check Mii Out Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Check_Mii_Out_Channel "Check Mii Out Channel"). The Wii can also communicate (and connect) with other Wii systems through a self-generated wireless [LAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_area_network "Local area network"), enabling local wireless multi-playing on different television sets. _[Battalion Wars 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battalion\_Wars\_2 "Battalion Wars 2")_ first demonstrated this feature for non-split screen multi-playing between two (or more) televisions.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-158)

### Third-party applications

Third-party media apps were added to the Wii's online channels, typically offered as free downloads but requiring subscriber logins for paid services. Among some of these included the [BBC iPlayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_iPlayer "BBC iPlayer") in November 2009,[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-159)[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-160)[Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") in November 2010,[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-161)[Hulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hulu "Hulu") in February 2012,[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-162)[YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") in December 2012,[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-163)[Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video") in January 2013,[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-164) and [Crunchyroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crunchyroll "Crunchyroll") in October 2015.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-165) In June 2017, YouTube ended support for its Wii channel.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-166) In January 2019, Nintendo ended support for all [streaming services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_service_provider "Streaming service provider") on the Wii.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wii_mini_disc-167)

### Parental controls

The console features [parental controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parental_controls "Parental controls"), which can be used to prohibit younger users from playing games with content unsuitable for their age level. When one attempts to play a Wii or Virtual Console game, it reads the content rating encoded in the game data; if this rating is greater than the system's set age level, the game will not load without a password. Parental controls may also restrict Internet access, which blocks the Internet Channel and system-update features. Since the console is restricted to GameCube functionality when playing GameCube Game Discs, GameCube software is unaffected by Wii parental-control settings.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-168)

The Wii also includes a system that records the playtime based on any game or app on the system. While Nintendo decided against a profile system that would require each user to identify themselves, they kept the cumulative playtime tracking system, which cannot be erased or altered, to give parents the means to review their children's use of the Wii.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii#cite_note-wired_wii_menu-147)

## Games
