The **Nintendo DS**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-6) is a foldable [handheld game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_game_console "Handheld game console") developed by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") and released worldwide between 2004 and 2005. The "DS" in the name is an [initialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initialism "Initialism") for "Dual Screen",[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-7) reflecting the system's most distinctive feature: two [LCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LCD "LCD") screens working in tandem, with the lower screen functioning as a [touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen "Touchscreen"). Both screens are housed in a [clamshell design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clamshell_design "Clamshell design") similar to that of the [Game Boy Advance SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_SP "Game Boy Advance SP") and some models of the [Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch "Game & Watch") series. The DS was among the first portable consoles to support [wireless connectivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_network "Wireless network") for local multiplayer over short distances, as well as online play through the now-defunct [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection") service.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-8) Its primary competitor during the [seventh generation of video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Seventh generation of video game consoles") was [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Interactive_Entertainment "Sony Interactive Entertainment")'s [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable").

Initially marketed as an experimental "third pillar" in Nintendo's console lineup—complementing the handheld [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") family and the home console [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube")—the DS's [backward compatibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility") with Game Boy Advance titles and strong sales led it to be widely regarded as the successor to the [Game Boy line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_family "Game Boy family").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-9) A slimmer model, the **Nintendo DS Lite**, which features brighter screens and improved battery life, was released in 2006.

The DS and DS Lite were followed by the [Nintendo DSi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DSi "Nintendo DSi"), a revision released on November 1, 2008. The DSi added dual [digital cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_camera "Digital camera"), larger screens, more memory, a faster processor, and internal flash memory, and it was later offered in a larger DSi XL model. It also introduced [digital distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") of games, but lost compatibility with Game Boy Advance cartridges. Although hundreds of downloadable titles were available, only six DSi-exclusive game cards were released. The DS line was ultimately succeeded by the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") in February 2011.

Including the DS Lite and DSi models, the Nintendo DS [has sold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_sales "Nintendo DS sales") 154 million units, becoming the best-selling [Nintendo console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_console "Nintendo console") until it was surpassed by the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch") in 2025. It also ranks as the [third best-selling video game console of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_game_consoles "List of best-selling game consoles"), behind the PlayStation 2 and the Switch. The DS Lite accounted for over 60 percent of total DS hardware shipments.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-sales-2)

## History

### Development

Development of the Nintendo DS began around mid-2002, as company president [Hiroshi Yamauchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshi_Yamauchi "Hiroshi Yamauchi") stepped down and assumed an advisory role. At the time, he proposed that Nintendo explore a system built around two screens.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

[Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata") succeeded Yamauchi as president in May 2002.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11) He acknowledged that Nintendo had fallen behind industry trends, particularly online gaming, and sought to broaden the company's audience beyond traditional gamers.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-IGN_iwata_bio-12) Internal research suggested that Nintendo's past emphasis on unconventional hardware had complicated third-party development and weakened its competitiveness.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-13) Iwata therefore supported development of a dual-screen handheld that would offer distinctive new ways to play, be more accessible to non-traditional audiences, and easier for developers to support. Because Nintendo believed consumers were unlikely to pay recurring fees for online services, the design emphasized wireless functionality to enable local multiplayer and new interactive experiences without subscriptions.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

On January 20, 2004, Nintendo announced that it would release a new dual-screen game device under the codename "Nintendo DS", describing it as an experimental "third pillar" alongside the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") and [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") rather than a replacement for either.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-janpress-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-newconsole-15) Few technical details were initially disclosed, other than that it would feature two 3-inch TFT LCD displays, dual processors, and up to 128 MB of memory.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-janpress-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-16)

In March 2004, a leaked document revealed additional technical specifications, including that one of the screens would be touch sensitive, and identified the internal development name "Nitro".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-17) The prototype was shown publicly in May at [E3 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2004 "E3 2004") in Los Angeles,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-18) where Nintendo of America president [Reggie Fils-Aimé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Fils-Aim%C3%A9 "Reggie Fils-Aimé") noted that the design would change before launch. On July 28, 2004, Nintendo unveiled a redesigned, "sleeker and more elegant" version and confirmed Nintendo DS as the final name.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-19)

Iwata characterized the DS as Nintendo's first hardware launch in support of its "Gaming Population Expansion" strategy, highlighting that its touch-based interface would allow for intuitive play, and described the project as "a completely different concept from existing game devices", intended to reassert the company's reputation for innovation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-janpress-14)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Message_from_the_President_Dec_2008-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-thirdpillar-21)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

In February 2004, while the Nintendo DS was still in development and amid concern over the GameCube's lukewarm performance, Yamauchi stated, "If the DS succeeds, we will rise to heaven, but if it fails we will sink to hell".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

### Launch

On September 20, 2004, Nintendo announced that the Nintendo DS would launch in North America on November 21, 2004, for [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")149.99(equivalent to $260 in 2025)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-22) followed by releases in Japan on December 2 for [¥](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_yen "Japanese yen")15,000(equivalent to ¥17,040 in 2024),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-JAPprice-23) in Australia and New Zealand on February 24, 2005, for [A$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_dollar "Australian dollar")199.95(equivalent to $310 in 2022) or [NZ$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_dollar "New Zealand dollar")249($420 in 2026),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-AUSprice-24) and in Europe on March 11, 2005, for [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro")149.99 or £99.99(equivalent to £180 in 2025).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-EURprice-25) The North American debut was marked by a midnight launch event in Los Angeles, while the Japanese launch was comparatively subdued, reportedly in part because of the winter weather.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-26)

Nintendo released the DS in North America ahead of Japan, its first hardware launch to follow that order, to position the system for the U.S. holiday shopping season and [Black Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Friday_(shopping) "Black Friday (shopping)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-27) Demand exceeded expectations: more than three million preorders were placed across North America and Japan, quickly exhausting many retailers' allocations. Nintendo initially planned to ship about one million units combined for both launches but added production capacity after seeing preorder volumes. For the U.S. launch, 550,000 units were shipped (up from a planned 300,000), with just over 500,000 sold in the first week. The system reached one million units sold in the United States by December 21, 2004, and worldwide shipments totaled 2.8 million by the end of the year—roughly 800,000 above Nintendo's forecast.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-28) By June 2005, global sales had reached 6.65 million units,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-29) and some commentators likened its popularity to the "[Tickle Me Elmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickle_Me_Elmo "Tickle Me Elmo")" craze of 1996.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-30)

Some early units were reported to have [stuck pixels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defective_pixel "Defective pixel"), as was common with LCD displays of the time. Nintendo of America launched a program to repair or replace screens if the owner felt that the stuck pixels interfered with their gaming experience.

#### China

The Nintendo DS was released in China on July 23, 2005, by Nintendo's [localization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_localization "Video game localization") partner [iQue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue "IQue") as the iQue DS. This version featured updated firmware to block [game piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_piracy "Video game piracy") and was also released in a new red color. Five games were localized for the system. The iQue DS is the only Nintendo DS model with regional lockout: games designed for it cannot be played on DS systems from other regions, although games from other regions are compatible with the iQue DS.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

### Promotion

The system's promotional slogans use the word "Touch" in almost all countries, with the North American slogan being "Touching is good."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-nbcnews-31)

The Nintendo DS was seen by many analysts to be in the same market as [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony "Sony")'s [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable"), although representatives from both companies stated that each system targeted a different audience.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-33)[_Time_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") awarded the DS a Gadget of the Week award.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-34)

At the time of its release in the United States, the Nintendo DS retailed for US$149.99. The price dropped to US$129.99 on August 21, 2005, one day before the release of _[Nintendogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendogs "Nintendogs")_ and _[Advance Wars: Dual Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advance\_Wars:\_Dual\_Strike "Advance Wars: Dual Strike")_.

Nine official colors of the Nintendo DS were available through standard retailers. Titanium-colored units were available worldwide; Electric Blue was exclusive to North and Latin America. There was also a red version which was bundled with the game _[Mario Kart DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_DS "Mario Kart DS")_. Graphite Black, Pure White, Turquoise Blue, and Candy Pink were available in Japan. Mystic Pink and Cosmic Blue[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-35) were available in Australia and New Zealand. Japan's Candy Pink and Australia's Cosmic Blue were also available in Europe and North America through a _Nintendogs_ bundle, although the colors are just referred to as pink and blue; however, these colors were available only for the original style Nintendo DS; a different and more-limited set of colors were used for the Nintendo DS Lite.

### DS Lite

"DS Lite" redirects here. For the IPv6 transition mechanism, see [DS-Lite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DS-Lite "DS-Lite").

[![Image 118](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Nintendo_DS_Compare.jpg/250px-Nintendo_DS_Compare.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_DS_Compare.jpg)

A Nintendo DS Lite (left) and an original DS (right)

The Nintendo DS Lite was announced on January 26, 2006,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-36) and showcased at [E3 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2006 "E3 2006") the following May.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-37) The system launched in Japan on March 2, 2006.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-reggie_interview-38) Heavy demand led to widespread shortages, and some retailers raised prices above [list price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_price "List price"). Nintendo shipped 550,000 units in March 2006, exceeding expectations, yet the console sold out quickly.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-reggie_interview-38) To address demand, the company shipped an additional 700,000 units in April, but retailers were again sold out by late May.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-39) Shortages continued through much of 2006 and 2007.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-soldout-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-41)

The DS Lite launched in Australia on June 1, 2006, bundled with a demo of _[Brain Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain\_Age:\_Train\_Your\_Brain\_in\_Minutes\_a\_Day! "Brain Age: Train Your Brain in Minutes a Day!")_.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-42) North America followed on June 11, 2006,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-litemario-43) with reports that some major chains sold units ahead of the official date.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-rumor_early-44) By June 12, most major U.S. retailers had sold out,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-US_sellout-45) and Nintendo reported sales of 136,500 units within the first two days.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-twodays-46)

In Europe, the DS Lite was released on June 23, 2006, with early launches in [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") and [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") to avoid the [Midsummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juhannus "Juhannus") holiday. Nintendo reported sales of 200,000 units across Europe in the first ten days.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-launch_Europe-47) During the launch period, a shipment of consoles and games valued at [HK$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_dollar "Hong Kong dollar")18 million (US$2.32 million, equivalent to 3.47 million in 2025) was stolen in [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") while in transit to Europe.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-49)

Following the establishment of Nintendo of Korea in July 2006, the DS Lite became the subsidiary's first console release on January 18, 2007.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-50) Promoted by actors [Jang Dong-gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jang_Dong-gun "Jang Dong-gun") and [Ahn Sung-ki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahn_Sung-ki "Ahn Sung-ki"), it sold more than one million units in South Korea within its first year, reaching 1.4 million by April 2008.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-51)

The Nintendo DS Lite was reportedly discontinued in April 2011.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-52)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-53)

### Sales

Main article: [Nintendo DS sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_sales "Nintendo DS sales")

As of March 31, 2016, all Nintendo DS models combined have sold 154.02 million units.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-nintendosales-10) The majority of these were made up of the first revision model, the DS Lite, according to Nintendo.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-nintendosales-10)

### Legacy

See also: [Nintendo DSi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DSi "Nintendo DSi") and [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS")

The Nintendo DS introduced [touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen "Touchscreen") controls and wireless [online gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_game "Online game") to a broad audience. Damien McFerran of _Nintendo Life_ wrote that the "DS was the first encounter many people had with touch-based tech, and it left an indelible impression."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-54) It established a large [casual gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casual_gaming "Casual gaming") market, attracting non-traditional gamers and setting touchscreens as a standard for future portable devices. Jeremy Parish, writing for _[Polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon\_(website) "Polygon (website)")_ stated that the DS, "had basically primed the entire world for" the iPhone (released in January 2007), laying the groundwork for touchscreen [mobile gaming apps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_game "Mobile game"), though he noted that the success of the iPhone "effectively caused the DS market to implode" by the early 2010s.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-55)

The DS also broadened the market for female gamers. In 2006, Nintendo reported that 44% of DS owners were female, with the majority of _[Nintendogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendogs "Nintendogs")_ players being women.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-56)

The system was followed by the Nintendo DSi, released on November 1, 2008, which added dual digital cameras and digital game distribution, while removing backward compatibility with Game Boy Advance titles. A larger variant, originally planned as a DS Lite variant, was released as the Nintendo DSi XL.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Briefing-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-fourth-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Christopher2009a-60)

The success of the DS also paved the way for the Nintendo 3DS, a dual-screen handheld capable of displaying stereoscopic 3D on the top screen.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Nintendo_to_unveil_3-D_gaming_console-61)

On January 29, 2014, Nintendo announced that DS games would be added to the [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")'s Virtual Console, with _Brain Age_ being the first released in Japan on June 3, 2014.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-62)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-VCJPrelease-63)

## Hardware

[![Image 119](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Nintendo-DS-Styli.jpg/250px-Nintendo-DS-Styli.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo-DS-Styli.jpg)

Stylus for the DS Lite

The design of the Nintendo DS recalls earlier Nintendo products, including the dual-screen series of the [Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch "Game & Watch") line—such as _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_(Game\_&\_Watch) "Donkey Kong (Game & Watch)")_ and _[Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zelda\_Game\_&\_Watch "Zelda Game & Watch")_—as well as the clamshell _[Game Boy Advance SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Boy\_Advance\_SP "Game Boy Advance SP")_.

The system uses two 3-inch (diagonal) [TFT LCDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TFT_LCD "TFT LCD"), each with a resolution of 256×192 pixels and a 4:3 [aspect ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_ratio "Aspect ratio"). The lower screen is covered by a [resistive touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistive_touchscreen "Resistive touchscreen") that accepts input from a finger or the included [stylus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylus_(computing) "Stylus (computing)"), which is stored in a holder on the device. The system also features a [D-pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-pad "D-pad") (referred to by Nintendo as the "+Control Pad"), six [action buttons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_button "Action button") on its front (A, B, X, Y, Start, and Select), and two [shoulder buttons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoulder_button "Shoulder button") (L and R). The overall layout resembles the [Super Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System") controller. The top edge houses the game card slot and power connector (the same as used with the [Game Boy Advance SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_SP "Game Boy Advance SP")), while the bottom includes the slot for [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") cartridges.

[Stereo speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereophonic_sound "Stereophonic sound")—positioned on either side of the upper display—can provide [virtual surround](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_surround "Virtual surround") sound. A built-in microphone sits below the lower screen and is used for features such as [speech recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition"), [voice chat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_chat_in_online_gaming "Voice chat in online gaming"), and gameplay actions that require the player to blow or shout into it.

The Nintendo DS contains two processors that operate together in an [asymmetric configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymmetric_multiprocessing "Asymmetric multiprocessing"). One is an [ARM7TDMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM7TDMI "ARM7TDMI")—the same as in the Game Boy Advance but clocked at twice the speed, 34 MHz—which handles input/output functions and provides backward compatibility with Game Boy Advance software. The second is an [ARM946E-S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM946E-S "ARM946E-S") running at 67 MHz, which performs most of the system's primary processing. The two processors share tasks and exchange data as required by software.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:1-64)

The console includes several types of memory: 32 kB of work RAM shared between both processors, an additional 64 kB accessible only to the ARM7, and 4 MB of [PSRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudostatic_RAM "Pseudostatic RAM") used as the main system memory. The system also contains 256 kB of flash memory that stores the firmware, user preferences, and certain system settings; firmware updates were not intended to be installed by the user.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:1-64)

The DS has 656 kB of video memory[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-65) and two 2D graphics engines (one for each screen), which are more capable than the single engine in the Game Boy Advance. The system's [3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics") hardware[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-problemkaputt.de-66) includes a geometry and rendering engine capable of effects such as [texture mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_mapping "Texture mapping"), [alpha blending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_blending "Alpha blending"), [Gouraud shading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouraud_shading "Gouraud shading"), [cel shading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cel_shading "Cel shading"), and basic lighting. Because it uses [nearest-neighbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest-neighbor_interpolation "Nearest-neighbor interpolation")[texture filtering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_filtering "Texture filtering"), some games appear blocky. It is also constrained by a fixed polygon budget—about 2,048 triangles per frame—and renders 3D to only one screen at a time, making dual-screen 3D difficult and performance-intensive. The DS also includes 512 kB of texture memory and supports textures up to 1024 × 1024 pixels.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-67)

The Nintendo DS supports [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi") via the [IEEE 802.11b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_802.11 "IEEE 802.11") standard, optionally with [WEP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired_Equivalent_Privacy "Wired Equivalent Privacy") encryption, enabling local multiplayer over short distances and online play through the now-defunct Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-69) These standards are now considered outdated, and WEP in particular is regarded as insecure.

Nintendo states that the rechargeable 850 mAh lithium-ion battery lasts up to 10 hours under ideal conditions after a 4-hour charge, though actual life depends on factors such as volume, screen brightness, wireless use, and whether one or both screens are active. The battery is user-replaceable with a Phillips screwdriver, and capacity declines after roughly 500 charge cycles.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-70)

Closing the system activates a sleep mode that pauses most games and conserves power by turning off the screens, speakers, and wireless features. Sleep mode does not function while playing Game Boy Advance titles, and some DS games do not pause.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-71) A few titles incorporate closing the system into gameplay.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-73)

### Nintendo DS Lite

The Nintendo DS Lite is a redesign of the Nintendo DS. While retaining the original model's core features, it features a slimmer case, a larger stylus, improved battery life, and brighter displays.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-74) The top screen has a maximum brightness of 200[cd/m 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candela_per_square_metre "Candela per square metre"), while the lower touch screen reaches 190 cd/m 2.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-75) Its 1000 mAh lithium-ion battery provides approximately 15–19 hours of play after about three hours of charging. The DS Lite uses a different AC adapter from the original Nintendo DS and the Game Boy Advance SP due to a smaller power port on the top of the unit.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-76) The included stylus is 1 cm longer and 2 mm thicker than that of the original model.

### Accessories

Main article: [Nintendo DS accessories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_accessories "Nintendo DS accessories")

Although the secondary port on the Nintendo DS accepts Game Boy Advance cartridges (but not Game Boy or Game Boy Color cartridges), Nintendo stated that its primary purpose was to support a range of accessories for the system.

#### Rumble Pak

Main article: [Rumble Pak §Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble_Pak#Nintendo_DS "Rumble Pak")

The Rumble Pak was the first accessory designed for the expansion slot. Shaped like a Game Boy Advance cartridge, it provides [force feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force_feedback "Force feedback") in compatible games. It was released in North America and Japan in 2005 bundled with _[Metroid Prime Pinball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metroid\_Prime\_Pinball "Metroid Prime Pinball")_.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-78) In Europe, it was first bundled with _[Actionloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetica "Magnetica")_ and later with _Metroid Prime Pinball_, and was also sold separately.

#### Headset

The Nintendo DS Headset is an official headset that connects to the combination headphone–microphone jack on the bottom of the system. It includes a single earphone and microphone and works with games that support voice input. It was released alongside [_Pokémon Diamond_ and _Pearl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Diamond_and_Pearl "Pokémon Diamond and Pearl") in North America and Australia.

#### Browser

Main article: [Nintendo DS Browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_Browser "Nintendo DS Browser")

On February 15, 2006, Nintendo announced a version of the [Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_(web_browser) "Opera (web browser)") web browser for the system.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Opera_PR-79) The browser can use one screen as an overview with a zoomed view on the other, or combine both screens into a single tall page view.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Opera_Berit-80) It was released in Japan and Europe in 2006 and in North America in 2007.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Opera_Japan-81)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-82)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-83) Operation requires the included memory expansion pak in the Game Boy Advance slot.

#### Wi-Fi USB Connector

Main article: [Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_USB_Connector "Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector")

This accessory connects to a PC's USB port and creates a small [wireless access point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_access_point "Wireless access point") in homes without Wi-Fi, allowing a Wii and up to five Nintendo DS systems to connect to the [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection") service through the host computer's Internet connection. The Wi-Fi USB Connector was eventually discontinued, and the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service ended in 2014.

#### Guitar grip controller

The Guitar Grip controller, bundled with _[Guitar Hero: On Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero:\_On\_Tour "Guitar Hero: On Tour")_, plugs into the GBA slot and features four buttons similar to those on full-size _[Guitar Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero "Guitar Hero")_ controllers. It includes a stylus shaped like a guitar pick and a hand strap, and ships with an adapter for the original Nintendo DS. The Guitar Grip is also compatible with _[Guitar Hero On Tour: Decades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero\_On\_Tour:\_Decades "Guitar Hero On Tour: Decades")_, _[Guitar Hero On Tour: Modern Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero\_On\_Tour:\_Modern\_Hits "Guitar Hero On Tour: Modern Hits")_, and _[Band Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band\_Hero#DS\_version "Band Hero")_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-84)

## Software and features

### Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection

Main article: [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection")

Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection was a free online game service run by Nintendo. Players with a compatible Nintendo DS game could connect to the service via a [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi") network using a [Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_USB_Connector "Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector") or a [wireless router](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_router "Wireless router"). The service was launched in North America, Australia, Japan and Europe throughout November 2005. An online compatible Nintendo DS game was released on the same day for each region.

### Download Play

See also: [Nintendo Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Zone "Nintendo Zone")

With Download Play, it is possible for users to play [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer_video_game "Multiplayer video game") games with other Nintendo DS systems, and later Nintendo 3DS systems, using only one game card. Players must have their systems within wireless range (up to approximately 65 feet) of each other for the guest system to download the necessary data from the host system. Only certain games supported this feature and usually played with much more limited features than the full game allowed.

Download Play is also utilized to migrate [Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon "Pokémon") from fourth generation games into the fifth generation [_Pokémon Black_ and _White_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Black_and_White "Pokémon Black and White"), an example of a task requiring two different game cards and two handheld units, but only one player.

Some Nintendo DS retailers featured [DS Download Stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DS_Download_Station "DS Download Station") that allowed users to download demos of current and upcoming DS games; however, due to memory limitations, the downloads were erased once the system was powered off. The Download Station was made up of 1 to 8 standard retail DS units, with a standard DS card containing the demo data. On May 7, 2008, Nintendo released the [Nintendo Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Menu "Wii Menu") for download on the Wii. The Nintendo Channel used WiiConnect24 to download Nintendo DS demos through it. From there, a user can select the demo they wish to play and, similar to the Nintendo DS Download Stations at retail outlets, download it to their DS and play it until it is powered off.

### Multi-Card Play

Multi-Card Play, like Download Play, allows users to play multiplayer games with other Nintendo DS systems. In this case, each system requires a game card. This mode is accessed from an in-game menu, rather than the normal DS menu.

### PictoChat

Main article: [PictoChat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PictoChat "PictoChat")

PictoChat allows users to communicate with other Nintendo DS users within local wireless range. Users can enter text (via an on-screen keyboard), handwrite messages or draw pictures (via the stylus and touchscreen). There are four chatrooms (A, B, C, D) in which people can go to chat. Up to sixteen people can connect in any one room.

PictoChat was not available for the subsequent Nintendo 3DS series of systems.

### Firmware

Nintendo's own [firmware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firmware "Firmware") boots the system. A health and safety warning is displayed first, then the main menu is loaded. The main menu presents the player with four main options to select: play a DS game, use PictoChat, initiate DS Download Play, or play a Game Boy Advance game. The main menu also has secondary options such as turning on or off the backlight, the system settings, and an alarm.

The firmware also features a clock, several options for customization (such as boot priority for when games are inserted and GBA screen preferences), and the ability to input user information and preferences (such as name, birthday, favorite color, etc.) that can be used in games.

Japanese,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-91) American,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-92) and European[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-93) consoles support the following languages: [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"), and [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language").

On consoles from mainland China, [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language") replaces Japanese, and on Korean consoles,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-94) Italian is replaced by [Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language").

### Compatibility

[![Image 133](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Game-Boy-Nintendo-DS-Slots.jpg/250px-Game-Boy-Nintendo-DS-Slots.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Game-Boy-Nintendo-DS-Slots.jpg)

[Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") game slot on Game Boy Advance SP (below) and Nintendo DS Lite (above)

[![Image 134](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Nintendo_Game_Cartridge_Size_Comparison.jpg/250px-Nintendo_Game_Cartridge_Size_Comparison.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_Game_Cartridge_Size_Comparison.jpg)

Clockwise from left: A [Game Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy "Game Boy") game cartridge, a [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") game cartridge, and a Nintendo DS game cartridge. On the far right is a [United States Nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel_(United_States_coin) "Nickel (United States coin)") shown for scale.

The Nintendo DS is [backward compatible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility") with [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") (GBA) cartridges. The smaller [Nintendo DS game cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Game_Card "Nintendo Game Card") fit into a slot on the top of the system, while Game Boy Advance games fit into a slot on the bottom. The Nintendo DS, like the [Game Boy Micro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Micro "Game Boy Micro"), is not backward compatible with games made for the original [Game Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy "Game Boy") and [Game Boy Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Color "Game Boy Color") because the required hardware is not included and the console has physical incompatibility with Game Boy and Game Boy Color games.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-95)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-96)

The handheld does not have a port for the Game Boy Advance Link Cable, so multiplayer and GameCube–Game Boy Advance link-up modes are not available in Game Boy Advance titles. Only single-player mode is supported on the Nintendo DS, as is the case with Game Boy Advance games played via the [Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console") on the Nintendo 3DS (Ambassadors only) and Wii U.

The Nintendo DS only uses one screen when playing Game Boy Advance games. The user can configure the system to use either the top or bottom screen by default. The games are displayed within a black border on the screen, due to the slightly different screen resolution between the two systems (256 × 192 px for the Nintendo DS, and 240 × 160 px for the Game Boy Advance).

Nintendo DS games inserted into the top slot are able to detect the presence of specific Game Boy Advance games in the bottom slot. In many such games, either stated in-game during gameplay or explained in its instruction manual, extra content can be unlocked or added by starting the Nintendo DS game with the appropriate Game Boy Advance game inserted. Among those games were the popular [_Pokémon Diamond_ and _Pearl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Diamond_and_Pearl "Pokémon Diamond and Pearl") or _[Pokémon Platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Platinum "Pokémon Platinum")_, which allowed the player to find more/exclusive Pokémon in the wild if a suitable Game Boy Advance cartridge was inserted. Some of the content can stay permanently, even after the GBA game has been removed.

Additionally, the GBA slot can be used to house expansion paks, such as the [Rumble Pak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nintendo_DS_Rumble_Pak_games "List of Nintendo DS Rumble Pak games"), [Nintendo DS Memory Expansion Pak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_Browser#DS_memory_expansion_pak "Nintendo DS Browser"), and Guitar Grips for the _[Guitar Hero: On Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero:\_On\_Tour\_series "Guitar Hero: On Tour series")_ series. The Nintendo DSi and the DSi XL have an SD card slot instead of a second cartridge slot and cannot play Game Boy Advance games or _[Guitar Hero: On Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero:\_On\_Tour\_series "Guitar Hero: On Tour series")_. In certain Wii games such as [Band Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_Hero "Band Hero"), the player can use a Nintendo DS for additional features.

### Regional division

The Nintendo DS is [region free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_lockout "Regional lockout") in the sense that any console will run a Nintendo DS game purchased anywhere in the world; however, the Chinese iQue DS games cannot be played on other versions of the original DS, whose firmware chip does not contain the required [Chinese character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_character "Chinese character") glyph images; this restriction is removed on Nintendo DSi and 3DS systems.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Although the Nintendo DS of other regions cannot play the Chinese games, the iQue DS can play games of other regions. Also, as with Game Boy games, some games that require both players to have a [Nintendo DS game card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_game_card "Nintendo DS game card") for multiplayer play will not necessarily work together if the games are from different regions (e.g. a Japanese Nintendo DS game may not work with a North American copy, even though some titles, such as _Mario Kart DS_ are mutually compatible). With the addition of the [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection"), certain games can be played over the Internet with users of a different region game.

Some Wi-Fi enabled games (e.g. _Mario Kart DS_) allow the selection of opponents by region. The options are "Regional" ("Continent" in Europe) and "Worldwide", as well as two non-location-specific settings. This allows the player to limit competitors to only those opponents based in the same geographical area. This is based on the region code of the game in use.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Media specifications

Main article: [Nintendo Game Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Game_Card "Nintendo Game Card")

Nintendo DS games use a proprietary [solid state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_state_(electronics) "Solid state (electronics)")[mask ROM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_ROM "Mask ROM") in their game cards.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-darkfader-97)[_[self-published source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Self-published\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The mask ROM chips are manufactured by Macronix and have an access time of 150[ns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanoseconds "Nanoseconds").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-gaingame-98)[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_] Cards range from 8 to 512[MiB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mebibyte "Mebibyte") (64[Mibit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mebibit "Mebibit") to 4[Gibit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibibit "Gibibit")) in size (although data on the maximum capacity has not been released).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-99)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-100) Larger cards have a 25% slower data transfer rate than more common smaller cards.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-101) The cards usually have a small amount of [flash memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_memory "Flash memory") or an [EEPROM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EEPROM "EEPROM") to save user data such as game progress or high scores. The game cards are 35 mm ×33 mm ×3.8 mm (1.38 in ×1.30 in ×0.15 in) (about half the width and depth of Game Boy Advance cartridges) and weigh around 3.5 g (1⁄8 oz).

## Hacking and homebrew

Main article: [Nintendo DS homebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_homebrew "Nintendo DS homebrew")

The [R4 cartridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R4_cartridge "R4 cartridge") (also known as Revolution for DS) is a popular [flash cartridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_cartridge "Flash cartridge") for the Nintendo DS. It allows ROMs and [homebrew games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homebrew_(video_games) "Homebrew (video games)") to be booted on the DS from a [microSD card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SD_card "SD card").

In South Korea, many video game consumers exploit illegal copies of video games, including those compatible with the DS. In 2007, over 500,000 copies of DS games were sold, while the sales of the DS hardware units was 800,000.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-102)

Another modification device called [Action Replay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_Replay "Action Replay"), manufactured by the company Datel, is a device which allows the user to input cheat codes that allows it to hack games, granting the player infinite [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_points "Health points"), [power-ups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power-ups "Power-ups"), access to any part of the game, infinite in game currency, the ability to walk through walls, and various other abilities depending on the game and code used.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-103)

The **Nintendo DS**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-6) is a foldable [handheld game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_game_console "Handheld game console") developed by [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") and released worldwide between 2004 and 2005. The "DS" in the name is an [initialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initialism "Initialism") for "Dual Screen",[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-7) reflecting the system's most distinctive feature: two [LCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LCD "LCD") screens working in tandem, with the lower screen functioning as a [touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen "Touchscreen"). Both screens are housed in a [clamshell design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clamshell_design "Clamshell design") similar to that of the [Game Boy Advance SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_SP "Game Boy Advance SP") and some models of the [Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch "Game & Watch") series. The DS was among the first portable consoles to support [wireless connectivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_network "Wireless network") for local multiplayer over short distances, as well as online play through the now-defunct [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection") service.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-8) Its primary competitor during the [seventh generation of video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Seventh generation of video game consoles") was [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Interactive_Entertainment "Sony Interactive Entertainment")'s [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable").

Initially marketed as an experimental "third pillar" in Nintendo's console lineup—complementing the handheld [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") family and the home console [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube")—the DS's [backward compatibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility") with Game Boy Advance titles and strong sales led it to be widely regarded as the successor to the [Game Boy line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_family "Game Boy family").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-9) A slimmer model, the **Nintendo DS Lite**, which features brighter screens and improved battery life, was released in 2006.

The DS and DS Lite were followed by the [Nintendo DSi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DSi "Nintendo DSi"), a revision released on November 1, 2008. The DSi added dual [digital cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_camera "Digital camera"), larger screens, more memory, a faster processor, and internal flash memory, and it was later offered in a larger DSi XL model. It also introduced [digital distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") of games, but lost compatibility with Game Boy Advance cartridges. Although hundreds of downloadable titles were available, only six DSi-exclusive game cards were released. The DS line was ultimately succeeded by the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") in February 2011.

Including the DS Lite and DSi models, the Nintendo DS [has sold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_sales "Nintendo DS sales") 154 million units, becoming the best-selling [Nintendo console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_console "Nintendo console") until it was surpassed by the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch") in 2025. It also ranks as the [third best-selling video game console of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_game_consoles "List of best-selling game consoles"), behind the PlayStation 2 and the Switch. The DS Lite accounted for over 60 percent of total DS hardware shipments.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-sales-2)

## History

### Development

Development of the Nintendo DS began around mid-2002, as company president [Hiroshi Yamauchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshi_Yamauchi "Hiroshi Yamauchi") stepped down and assumed an advisory role. At the time, he proposed that Nintendo explore a system built around two screens.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

[Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata") succeeded Yamauchi as president in May 2002.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11) He acknowledged that Nintendo had fallen behind industry trends, particularly online gaming, and sought to broaden the company's audience beyond traditional gamers.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-IGN_iwata_bio-12) Internal research suggested that Nintendo's past emphasis on unconventional hardware had complicated third-party development and weakened its competitiveness.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-13) Iwata therefore supported development of a dual-screen handheld that would offer distinctive new ways to play, be more accessible to non-traditional audiences, and easier for developers to support. Because Nintendo believed consumers were unlikely to pay recurring fees for online services, the design emphasized wireless functionality to enable local multiplayer and new interactive experiences without subscriptions.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

On January 20, 2004, Nintendo announced that it would release a new dual-screen game device under the codename "Nintendo DS", describing it as an experimental "third pillar" alongside the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") and [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") rather than a replacement for either.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-janpress-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-newconsole-15) Few technical details were initially disclosed, other than that it would feature two 3-inch TFT LCD displays, dual processors, and up to 128 MB of memory.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-janpress-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-16)

In March 2004, a leaked document revealed additional technical specifications, including that one of the screens would be touch sensitive, and identified the internal development name "Nitro".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-17) The prototype was shown publicly in May at [E3 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2004 "E3 2004") in Los Angeles,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-18) where Nintendo of America president [Reggie Fils-Aimé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Fils-Aim%C3%A9 "Reggie Fils-Aimé") noted that the design would change before launch. On July 28, 2004, Nintendo unveiled a redesigned, "sleeker and more elegant" version and confirmed Nintendo DS as the final name.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-19)

Iwata characterized the DS as Nintendo's first hardware launch in support of its "Gaming Population Expansion" strategy, highlighting that its touch-based interface would allow for intuitive play, and described the project as "a completely different concept from existing game devices", intended to reassert the company's reputation for innovation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-janpress-14)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Message_from_the_President_Dec_2008-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-thirdpillar-21)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

In February 2004, while the Nintendo DS was still in development and amid concern over the GameCube's lukewarm performance, Yamauchi stated, "If the DS succeeds, we will rise to heaven, but if it fails we will sink to hell".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

### Launch

On September 20, 2004, Nintendo announced that the Nintendo DS would launch in North America on November 21, 2004, for [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")149.99(equivalent to $260 in 2025)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-22) followed by releases in Japan on December 2 for [¥](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_yen "Japanese yen")15,000(equivalent to ¥17,040 in 2024),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-JAPprice-23) in Australia and New Zealand on February 24, 2005, for [A$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_dollar "Australian dollar")199.95(equivalent to $310 in 2022) or [NZ$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_dollar "New Zealand dollar")249($420 in 2026),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-AUSprice-24) and in Europe on March 11, 2005, for [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro")149.99 or £99.99(equivalent to £180 in 2025).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-EURprice-25) The North American debut was marked by a midnight launch event in Los Angeles, while the Japanese launch was comparatively subdued, reportedly in part because of the winter weather.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-26)

Nintendo released the DS in North America ahead of Japan, its first hardware launch to follow that order, to position the system for the U.S. holiday shopping season and [Black Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Friday_(shopping) "Black Friday (shopping)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-27) Demand exceeded expectations: more than three million preorders were placed across North America and Japan, quickly exhausting many retailers' allocations. Nintendo initially planned to ship about one million units combined for both launches but added production capacity after seeing preorder volumes. For the U.S. launch, 550,000 units were shipped (up from a planned 300,000), with just over 500,000 sold in the first week. The system reached one million units sold in the United States by December 21, 2004, and worldwide shipments totaled 2.8 million by the end of the year—roughly 800,000 above Nintendo's forecast.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-28) By June 2005, global sales had reached 6.65 million units,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-29) and some commentators likened its popularity to the "[Tickle Me Elmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tickle_Me_Elmo "Tickle Me Elmo")" craze of 1996.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-30)

Some early units were reported to have [stuck pixels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defective_pixel "Defective pixel"), as was common with LCD displays of the time. Nintendo of America launched a program to repair or replace screens if the owner felt that the stuck pixels interfered with their gaming experience.

#### China

The Nintendo DS was released in China on July 23, 2005, by Nintendo's [localization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_localization "Video game localization") partner [iQue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue "IQue") as the iQue DS. This version featured updated firmware to block [game piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_piracy "Video game piracy") and was also released in a new red color. Five games were localized for the system. The iQue DS is the only Nintendo DS model with regional lockout: games designed for it cannot be played on DS systems from other regions, although games from other regions are compatible with the iQue DS.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:0-11)

### Promotion

The system's promotional slogans use the word "Touch" in almost all countries, with the North American slogan being "Touching is good."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-nbcnews-31)

The Nintendo DS was seen by many analysts to be in the same market as [Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony "Sony")'s [PlayStation Portable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Portable "PlayStation Portable"), although representatives from both companies stated that each system targeted a different audience.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-33)[_Time_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") awarded the DS a Gadget of the Week award.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-34)

At the time of its release in the United States, the Nintendo DS retailed for US$149.99. The price dropped to US$129.99 on August 21, 2005, one day before the release of _[Nintendogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendogs "Nintendogs")_ and _[Advance Wars: Dual Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advance\_Wars:\_Dual\_Strike "Advance Wars: Dual Strike")_.

Nine official colors of the Nintendo DS were available through standard retailers. Titanium-colored units were available worldwide; Electric Blue was exclusive to North and Latin America. There was also a red version which was bundled with the game _[Mario Kart DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_DS "Mario Kart DS")_. Graphite Black, Pure White, Turquoise Blue, and Candy Pink were available in Japan. Mystic Pink and Cosmic Blue[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-35) were available in Australia and New Zealand. Japan's Candy Pink and Australia's Cosmic Blue were also available in Europe and North America through a _Nintendogs_ bundle, although the colors are just referred to as pink and blue; however, these colors were available only for the original style Nintendo DS; a different and more-limited set of colors were used for the Nintendo DS Lite.

### DS Lite

"DS Lite" redirects here. For the IPv6 transition mechanism, see [DS-Lite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DS-Lite "DS-Lite").

[![Image 118](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Nintendo_DS_Compare.jpg/250px-Nintendo_DS_Compare.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_DS_Compare.jpg)

A Nintendo DS Lite (left) and an original DS (right)

The Nintendo DS Lite was announced on January 26, 2006,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-36) and showcased at [E3 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2006 "E3 2006") the following May.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-37) The system launched in Japan on March 2, 2006.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-reggie_interview-38) Heavy demand led to widespread shortages, and some retailers raised prices above [list price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_price "List price"). Nintendo shipped 550,000 units in March 2006, exceeding expectations, yet the console sold out quickly.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-reggie_interview-38) To address demand, the company shipped an additional 700,000 units in April, but retailers were again sold out by late May.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-39) Shortages continued through much of 2006 and 2007.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-soldout-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-41)

The DS Lite launched in Australia on June 1, 2006, bundled with a demo of _[Brain Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain\_Age:\_Train\_Your\_Brain\_in\_Minutes\_a\_Day! "Brain Age: Train Your Brain in Minutes a Day!")_.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-42) North America followed on June 11, 2006,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-litemario-43) with reports that some major chains sold units ahead of the official date.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-rumor_early-44) By June 12, most major U.S. retailers had sold out,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-US_sellout-45) and Nintendo reported sales of 136,500 units within the first two days.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-twodays-46)

In Europe, the DS Lite was released on June 23, 2006, with early launches in [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") and [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") to avoid the [Midsummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juhannus "Juhannus") holiday. Nintendo reported sales of 200,000 units across Europe in the first ten days.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-launch_Europe-47) During the launch period, a shipment of consoles and games valued at [HK$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_dollar "Hong Kong dollar")18 million (US$2.32 million, equivalent to 3.47 million in 2025) was stolen in [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") while in transit to Europe.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-49)

Following the establishment of Nintendo of Korea in July 2006, the DS Lite became the subsidiary's first console release on January 18, 2007.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-50) Promoted by actors [Jang Dong-gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jang_Dong-gun "Jang Dong-gun") and [Ahn Sung-ki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahn_Sung-ki "Ahn Sung-ki"), it sold more than one million units in South Korea within its first year, reaching 1.4 million by April 2008.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-51)

The Nintendo DS Lite was reportedly discontinued in April 2011.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-52)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-53)

### Sales

Main article: [Nintendo DS sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_sales "Nintendo DS sales")

As of March 31, 2016, all Nintendo DS models combined have sold 154.02 million units.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-nintendosales-10) The majority of these were made up of the first revision model, the DS Lite, according to Nintendo.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-nintendosales-10)

### Legacy

See also: [Nintendo DSi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DSi "Nintendo DSi") and [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS")

The Nintendo DS introduced [touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchscreen "Touchscreen") controls and wireless [online gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_game "Online game") to a broad audience. Damien McFerran of _Nintendo Life_ wrote that the "DS was the first encounter many people had with touch-based tech, and it left an indelible impression."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-54) It established a large [casual gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casual_gaming "Casual gaming") market, attracting non-traditional gamers and setting touchscreens as a standard for future portable devices. Jeremy Parish, writing for _[Polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon\_(website) "Polygon (website)")_ stated that the DS, "had basically primed the entire world for" the iPhone (released in January 2007), laying the groundwork for touchscreen [mobile gaming apps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_game "Mobile game"), though he noted that the success of the iPhone "effectively caused the DS market to implode" by the early 2010s.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-55)

The DS also broadened the market for female gamers. In 2006, Nintendo reported that 44% of DS owners were female, with the majority of _[Nintendogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendogs "Nintendogs")_ players being women.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-56)

The system was followed by the Nintendo DSi, released on November 1, 2008, which added dual digital cameras and digital game distribution, while removing backward compatibility with Game Boy Advance titles. A larger variant, originally planned as a DS Lite variant, was released as the Nintendo DSi XL.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Briefing-58)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-fourth-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Christopher2009a-60)

The success of the DS also paved the way for the Nintendo 3DS, a dual-screen handheld capable of displaying stereoscopic 3D on the top screen.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Nintendo_to_unveil_3-D_gaming_console-61)

On January 29, 2014, Nintendo announced that DS games would be added to the [Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_U "Wii U")'s Virtual Console, with _Brain Age_ being the first released in Japan on June 3, 2014.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-62)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-VCJPrelease-63)

## Hardware

[![Image 119](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Nintendo-DS-Styli.jpg/250px-Nintendo-DS-Styli.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo-DS-Styli.jpg)

Stylus for the DS Lite

The design of the Nintendo DS recalls earlier Nintendo products, including the dual-screen series of the [Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch "Game & Watch") line—such as _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_(Game\_&\_Watch) "Donkey Kong (Game & Watch)")_ and _[Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zelda\_Game\_&\_Watch "Zelda Game & Watch")_—as well as the clamshell _[Game Boy Advance SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Boy\_Advance\_SP "Game Boy Advance SP")_.

The system uses two 3-inch (diagonal) [TFT LCDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TFT_LCD "TFT LCD"), each with a resolution of 256×192 pixels and a 4:3 [aspect ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_ratio "Aspect ratio"). The lower screen is covered by a [resistive touchscreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistive_touchscreen "Resistive touchscreen") that accepts input from a finger or the included [stylus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylus_(computing) "Stylus (computing)"), which is stored in a holder on the device. The system also features a [D-pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-pad "D-pad") (referred to by Nintendo as the "+Control Pad"), six [action buttons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_button "Action button") on its front (A, B, X, Y, Start, and Select), and two [shoulder buttons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoulder_button "Shoulder button") (L and R). The overall layout resembles the [Super Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System") controller. The top edge houses the game card slot and power connector (the same as used with the [Game Boy Advance SP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_SP "Game Boy Advance SP")), while the bottom includes the slot for [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") cartridges.

[Stereo speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereophonic_sound "Stereophonic sound")—positioned on either side of the upper display—can provide [virtual surround](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_surround "Virtual surround") sound. A built-in microphone sits below the lower screen and is used for features such as [speech recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition"), [voice chat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_chat_in_online_gaming "Voice chat in online gaming"), and gameplay actions that require the player to blow or shout into it.

The Nintendo DS contains two processors that operate together in an [asymmetric configuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymmetric_multiprocessing "Asymmetric multiprocessing"). One is an [ARM7TDMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM7TDMI "ARM7TDMI")—the same as in the Game Boy Advance but clocked at twice the speed, 34 MHz—which handles input/output functions and provides backward compatibility with Game Boy Advance software. The second is an [ARM946E-S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM946E-S "ARM946E-S") running at 67 MHz, which performs most of the system's primary processing. The two processors share tasks and exchange data as required by software.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:1-64)

The console includes several types of memory: 32 kB of work RAM shared between both processors, an additional 64 kB accessible only to the ARM7, and 4 MB of [PSRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudostatic_RAM "Pseudostatic RAM") used as the main system memory. The system also contains 256 kB of flash memory that stores the firmware, user preferences, and certain system settings; firmware updates were not intended to be installed by the user.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-:1-64)

The DS has 656 kB of video memory[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-65) and two 2D graphics engines (one for each screen), which are more capable than the single engine in the Game Boy Advance. The system's [3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_computer_graphics "3D computer graphics") hardware[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-problemkaputt.de-66) includes a geometry and rendering engine capable of effects such as [texture mapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_mapping "Texture mapping"), [alpha blending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_blending "Alpha blending"), [Gouraud shading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouraud_shading "Gouraud shading"), [cel shading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cel_shading "Cel shading"), and basic lighting. Because it uses [nearest-neighbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nearest-neighbor_interpolation "Nearest-neighbor interpolation")[texture filtering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_filtering "Texture filtering"), some games appear blocky. It is also constrained by a fixed polygon budget—about 2,048 triangles per frame—and renders 3D to only one screen at a time, making dual-screen 3D difficult and performance-intensive. The DS also includes 512 kB of texture memory and supports textures up to 1024 × 1024 pixels.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-67)

The Nintendo DS supports [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi") via the [IEEE 802.11b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_802.11 "IEEE 802.11") standard, optionally with [WEP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired_Equivalent_Privacy "Wired Equivalent Privacy") encryption, enabling local multiplayer over short distances and online play through the now-defunct Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-69) These standards are now considered outdated, and WEP in particular is regarded as insecure.

Nintendo states that the rechargeable 850 mAh lithium-ion battery lasts up to 10 hours under ideal conditions after a 4-hour charge, though actual life depends on factors such as volume, screen brightness, wireless use, and whether one or both screens are active. The battery is user-replaceable with a Phillips screwdriver, and capacity declines after roughly 500 charge cycles.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-70)

Closing the system activates a sleep mode that pauses most games and conserves power by turning off the screens, speakers, and wireless features. Sleep mode does not function while playing Game Boy Advance titles, and some DS games do not pause.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-71) A few titles incorporate closing the system into gameplay.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-73)

### Nintendo DS Lite

The Nintendo DS Lite is a redesign of the Nintendo DS. While retaining the original model's core features, it features a slimmer case, a larger stylus, improved battery life, and brighter displays.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-74) The top screen has a maximum brightness of 200[cd/m 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candela_per_square_metre "Candela per square metre"), while the lower touch screen reaches 190 cd/m 2.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-75) Its 1000 mAh lithium-ion battery provides approximately 15–19 hours of play after about three hours of charging. The DS Lite uses a different AC adapter from the original Nintendo DS and the Game Boy Advance SP due to a smaller power port on the top of the unit.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-76) The included stylus is 1 cm longer and 2 mm thicker than that of the original model.
