### Accessories

Main article: [Nintendo DS accessories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_accessories "Nintendo DS accessories")

Although the secondary port on the Nintendo DS accepts Game Boy Advance cartridges (but not Game Boy or Game Boy Color cartridges), Nintendo stated that its primary purpose was to support a range of accessories for the system.

#### Rumble Pak

Main article: [Rumble Pak §Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble_Pak#Nintendo_DS "Rumble Pak")

The Rumble Pak was the first accessory designed for the expansion slot. Shaped like a Game Boy Advance cartridge, it provides [force feedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force_feedback "Force feedback") in compatible games. It was released in North America and Japan in 2005 bundled with _[Metroid Prime Pinball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metroid\_Prime\_Pinball "Metroid Prime Pinball")_.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-78) In Europe, it was first bundled with _[Actionloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetica "Magnetica")_ and later with _Metroid Prime Pinball_, and was also sold separately.

#### Headset

The Nintendo DS Headset is an official headset that connects to the combination headphone–microphone jack on the bottom of the system. It includes a single earphone and microphone and works with games that support voice input. It was released alongside [_Pokémon Diamond_ and _Pearl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Diamond_and_Pearl "Pokémon Diamond and Pearl") in North America and Australia.

#### Browser

Main article: [Nintendo DS Browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_Browser "Nintendo DS Browser")

On February 15, 2006, Nintendo announced a version of the [Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_(web_browser) "Opera (web browser)") web browser for the system.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Opera_PR-79) The browser can use one screen as an overview with a zoomed view on the other, or combine both screens into a single tall page view.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Opera_Berit-80) It was released in Japan and Europe in 2006 and in North America in 2007.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-Opera_Japan-81)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-82)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-83) Operation requires the included memory expansion pak in the Game Boy Advance slot.

#### Wi-Fi USB Connector

Main article: [Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_USB_Connector "Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector")

This accessory connects to a PC's USB port and creates a small [wireless access point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_access_point "Wireless access point") in homes without Wi-Fi, allowing a Wii and up to five Nintendo DS systems to connect to the [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection") service through the host computer's Internet connection. The Wi-Fi USB Connector was eventually discontinued, and the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service ended in 2014.

#### Guitar grip controller

The Guitar Grip controller, bundled with _[Guitar Hero: On Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero:\_On\_Tour "Guitar Hero: On Tour")_, plugs into the GBA slot and features four buttons similar to those on full-size _[Guitar Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero "Guitar Hero")_ controllers. It includes a stylus shaped like a guitar pick and a hand strap, and ships with an adapter for the original Nintendo DS. The Guitar Grip is also compatible with _[Guitar Hero On Tour: Decades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero\_On\_Tour:\_Decades "Guitar Hero On Tour: Decades")_, _[Guitar Hero On Tour: Modern Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero\_On\_Tour:\_Modern\_Hits "Guitar Hero On Tour: Modern Hits")_, and _[Band Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band\_Hero#DS\_version "Band Hero")_.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-84)

## Software and features

### Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection

Main article: [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection")

Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection was a free online game service run by Nintendo. Players with a compatible Nintendo DS game could connect to the service via a [Wi-Fi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi "Wi-Fi") network using a [Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_USB_Connector "Nintendo Wi-Fi USB Connector") or a [wireless router](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_router "Wireless router"). The service was launched in North America, Australia, Japan and Europe throughout November 2005. An online compatible Nintendo DS game was released on the same day for each region.

### Download Play

See also: [Nintendo Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Zone "Nintendo Zone")

With Download Play, it is possible for users to play [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer_video_game "Multiplayer video game") games with other Nintendo DS systems, and later Nintendo 3DS systems, using only one game card. Players must have their systems within wireless range (up to approximately 65 feet) of each other for the guest system to download the necessary data from the host system. Only certain games supported this feature and usually played with much more limited features than the full game allowed.

Download Play is also utilized to migrate [Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon "Pokémon") from fourth generation games into the fifth generation [_Pokémon Black_ and _White_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Black_and_White "Pokémon Black and White"), an example of a task requiring two different game cards and two handheld units, but only one player.

Some Nintendo DS retailers featured [DS Download Stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DS_Download_Station "DS Download Station") that allowed users to download demos of current and upcoming DS games; however, due to memory limitations, the downloads were erased once the system was powered off. The Download Station was made up of 1 to 8 standard retail DS units, with a standard DS card containing the demo data. On May 7, 2008, Nintendo released the [Nintendo Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii_Menu "Wii Menu") for download on the Wii. The Nintendo Channel used WiiConnect24 to download Nintendo DS demos through it. From there, a user can select the demo they wish to play and, similar to the Nintendo DS Download Stations at retail outlets, download it to their DS and play it until it is powered off.

### Multi-Card Play

Multi-Card Play, like Download Play, allows users to play multiplayer games with other Nintendo DS systems. In this case, each system requires a game card. This mode is accessed from an in-game menu, rather than the normal DS menu.

### PictoChat

Main article: [PictoChat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PictoChat "PictoChat")

PictoChat allows users to communicate with other Nintendo DS users within local wireless range. Users can enter text (via an on-screen keyboard), handwrite messages or draw pictures (via the stylus and touchscreen). There are four chatrooms (A, B, C, D) in which people can go to chat. Up to sixteen people can connect in any one room.

PictoChat was not available for the subsequent Nintendo 3DS series of systems.

### Firmware

Nintendo's own [firmware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firmware "Firmware") boots the system. A health and safety warning is displayed first, then the main menu is loaded. The main menu presents the player with four main options to select: play a DS game, use PictoChat, initiate DS Download Play, or play a Game Boy Advance game. The main menu also has secondary options such as turning on or off the backlight, the system settings, and an alarm.

The firmware also features a clock, several options for customization (such as boot priority for when games are inserted and GBA screen preferences), and the ability to input user information and preferences (such as name, birthday, favorite color, etc.) that can be used in games.

Japanese,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-91) American,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-92) and European[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-93) consoles support the following languages: [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"), and [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language").

### Compatibility

[![Image 133](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Game-Boy-Nintendo-DS-Slots.jpg/250px-Game-Boy-Nintendo-DS-Slots.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Game-Boy-Nintendo-DS-Slots.jpg)

[Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") game slot on Game Boy Advance SP (below) and Nintendo DS Lite (above)

[![Image 134](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Nintendo_Game_Cartridge_Size_Comparison.jpg/250px-Nintendo_Game_Cartridge_Size_Comparison.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_Game_Cartridge_Size_Comparison.jpg)

Clockwise from left: A [Game Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy "Game Boy") game cartridge, a [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") game cartridge, and a Nintendo DS game cartridge. On the far right is a [United States Nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickel_(United_States_coin) "Nickel (United States coin)") shown for scale.

The Nintendo DS is [backward compatible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility") with [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") (GBA) cartridges. The smaller [Nintendo DS game cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Game_Card "Nintendo Game Card") fit into a slot on the top of the system, while Game Boy Advance games fit into a slot on the bottom. The Nintendo DS, like the [Game Boy Micro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Micro "Game Boy Micro"), is not backward compatible with games made for the original [Game Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy "Game Boy") and [Game Boy Color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Color "Game Boy Color") because the required hardware is not included and the console has physical incompatibility with Game Boy and Game Boy Color games.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-95)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-96)

The handheld does not have a port for the Game Boy Advance Link Cable, so multiplayer and GameCube–Game Boy Advance link-up modes are not available in Game Boy Advance titles. Only single-player mode is supported on the Nintendo DS, as is the case with Game Boy Advance games played via the [Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console") on the Nintendo 3DS (Ambassadors only) and Wii U.

The Nintendo DS only uses one screen when playing Game Boy Advance games. The user can configure the system to use either the top or bottom screen by default. The games are displayed within a black border on the screen, due to the slightly different screen resolution between the two systems (256 × 192 px for the Nintendo DS, and 240 × 160 px for the Game Boy Advance).

Nintendo DS games inserted into the top slot are able to detect the presence of specific Game Boy Advance games in the bottom slot. In many such games, either stated in-game during gameplay or explained in its instruction manual, extra content can be unlocked or added by starting the Nintendo DS game with the appropriate Game Boy Advance game inserted. Among those games were the popular [_Pokémon Diamond_ and _Pearl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Diamond_and_Pearl "Pokémon Diamond and Pearl") or _[Pokémon Platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Platinum "Pokémon Platinum")_, which allowed the player to find more/exclusive Pokémon in the wild if a suitable Game Boy Advance cartridge was inserted. Some of the content can stay permanently, even after the GBA game has been removed.

Additionally, the GBA slot can be used to house expansion paks, such as the [Rumble Pak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nintendo_DS_Rumble_Pak_games "List of Nintendo DS Rumble Pak games"), [Nintendo DS Memory Expansion Pak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_Browser#DS_memory_expansion_pak "Nintendo DS Browser"), and Guitar Grips for the _[Guitar Hero: On Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero:\_On\_Tour\_series "Guitar Hero: On Tour series")_ series. The Nintendo DSi and the DSi XL have an SD card slot instead of a second cartridge slot and cannot play Game Boy Advance games or _[Guitar Hero: On Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar\_Hero:\_On\_Tour\_series "Guitar Hero: On Tour series")_. In certain Wii games such as [Band Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Band_Hero "Band Hero"), the player can use a Nintendo DS for additional features.

### Regional division

The Nintendo DS is [region free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_lockout "Regional lockout") in the sense that any console will run a Nintendo DS game purchased anywhere in the world; however, the Chinese iQue DS games cannot be played on other versions of the original DS, whose firmware chip does not contain the required [Chinese character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_character "Chinese character") glyph images; this restriction is removed on Nintendo DSi and 3DS systems.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Although the Nintendo DS of other regions cannot play the Chinese games, the iQue DS can play games of other regions. Also, as with Game Boy games, some games that require both players to have a [Nintendo DS game card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_game_card "Nintendo DS game card") for multiplayer play will not necessarily work together if the games are from different regions (e.g. a Japanese Nintendo DS game may not work with a North American copy, even though some titles, such as _Mario Kart DS_ are mutually compatible). With the addition of the [Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Wi-Fi_Connection "Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection"), certain games can be played over the Internet with users of a different region game.

Some Wi-Fi enabled games (e.g. _Mario Kart DS_) allow the selection of opponents by region. The options are "Regional" ("Continent" in Europe) and "Worldwide", as well as two non-location-specific settings. This allows the player to limit competitors to only those opponents based in the same geographical area. This is based on the region code of the game in use.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Media specifications

Main article: [Nintendo Game Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Game_Card "Nintendo Game Card")

Nintendo DS games use a proprietary [solid state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_state_(electronics) "Solid state (electronics)")[mask ROM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_ROM "Mask ROM") in their game cards.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-darkfader-97)[_[self-published source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Self-published\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The mask ROM chips are manufactured by Macronix and have an access time of 150[ns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanoseconds "Nanoseconds").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-gaingame-98)[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_] Cards range from 8 to 512[MiB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mebibyte "Mebibyte") (64[Mibit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mebibit "Mebibit") to 4[Gibit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibibit "Gibibit")) in size (although data on the maximum capacity has not been released).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-99)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-100) Larger cards have a 25% slower data transfer rate than more common smaller cards.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-101) The cards usually have a small amount of [flash memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_memory "Flash memory") or an [EEPROM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EEPROM "EEPROM") to save user data such as game progress or high scores. The game cards are 35 mm ×33 mm ×3.8 mm (1.38 in ×1.30 in ×0.15 in) (about half the width and depth of Game Boy Advance cartridges) and weigh around 3.5 g (1⁄8 oz).

## Hacking and homebrew

Main article: [Nintendo DS homebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS_homebrew "Nintendo DS homebrew")

The [R4 cartridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R4_cartridge "R4 cartridge") (also known as Revolution for DS) is a popular [flash cartridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_cartridge "Flash cartridge") for the Nintendo DS. It allows ROMs and [homebrew games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homebrew_(video_games) "Homebrew (video games)") to be booted on the DS from a [microSD card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SD_card "SD card").

In South Korea, many video game consumers exploit illegal copies of video games, including those compatible with the DS. In 2007, over 500,000 copies of DS games were sold, while the sales of the DS hardware units was 800,000.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-102)

Another modification device called [Action Replay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_Replay "Action Replay"), manufactured by the company Datel, is a device which allows the user to input cheat codes that allows it to hack games, granting the player infinite [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_points "Health points"), [power-ups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power-ups "Power-ups"), access to any part of the game, infinite in game currency, the ability to walk through walls, and various other abilities depending on the game and code used.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS#cite_note-103)

**Nintendo Co., Ltd.**[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-9) is a Japanese [multinational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") video game company headquartered in [Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto"). It develops, publishes, and manufactures both [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") and [video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console "Video game console").

The [history of Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Nintendo "History of Nintendo") began when craftsman [Fusajiro Yamauchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusajiro_Yamauchi "Fusajiro Yamauchi") founded the company in 1889 to produce handmade _[hanafuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanafuda "Hanafuda")_ playing cards. After venturing into various lines of business and becoming a public company, Nintendo began producing toys in the 1960s, and later video games. Nintendo developed its first [arcade games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game") in the 1970s, and distributed its first system, the [Color TV-Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_TV-Game "Color TV-Game") in 1977. The company became internationally dominant in the 1980s after the arcade release of _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_(1981\_video\_game) "Donkey Kong (1981 video game)")_ (1981) and the [Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Nintendo Entertainment System"), which launched outside of Japan alongside _[Super Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Bros. "Super Mario Bros.")_ in 1985.

Since then, Nintendo has produced some of the most successful consoles in the [video game industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_industry "Video game industry"), including the [Game Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy "Game Boy") (1989), the [Super Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System") (1991), the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") (2001), the Nintendo DS (2004), the Wii (2006), and the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch") (2017). It has created or published [numerous major franchises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nintendo_franchises "List of Nintendo franchises"), including _[Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_(franchise) "Mario (franchise)")_, _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong "Donkey Kong")_, _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda "The Legend of Zelda")_, _[Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon "Pokémon")_, _[Super Smash Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros. "Super Smash Bros.")_, _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_, _[Splatoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splatoon "Splatoon"),_ _[Metroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metroid "Metroid")_, _[Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirby\_(series) "Kirby (series)")_, and _[Star Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Fox "Star Fox")_. The company's mascot, [Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario "Mario"), is among the most famous fictional characters, and Nintendo's [other characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_characters "Nintendo characters")—including [Luigi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_(character) "Luigi (character)"), [Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey_Kong_(character) "Donkey Kong (character)"), [Samus Aran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samus_Aran "Samus Aran"), [Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link_(The_Legend_of_Zelda) "Link (The Legend of Zelda)"), [Kirby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirby_(character) "Kirby (character)"), [Pikachu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pikachu "Pikachu"), and [Fox McCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_McCloud "Fox McCloud")—have attained international recognition. Several films and [a theme park area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_World "Super Nintendo World") based on the company's franchises have been created.

[Nintendo's game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_video_game_consoles "Nintendo video game consoles") have sold over 860 million units worldwide as of May 2025, for which more than 5.9 billion individual games have been sold. The company has [numerous subsidiaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nintendo_development_teams "List of Nintendo development teams") in Japan and worldwide, in addition to [second-party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_party_developer "Second party developer") developers including [HAL Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HAL_Laboratory "HAL Laboratory"), [Intelligent Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligent_Systems "Intelligent Systems"), and [Game Freak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Freak "Game Freak"). It is one of the wealthiest and most valuable companies in the Japanese market.

## History

Main article: [History of Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Nintendo "History of Nintendo")

### Early history

#### 1889–1932: Origin as a playing card business

[![Image 14: 1889–1933, in Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Nintendo_1889.jpg/250px-Nintendo_1889.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_1889.jpg)

Original Nintendo headquarters (1889–1930) and workshop in [Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimogy%C5%8D-ku,_Kyoto "Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto"), c.1889. The right section was eventually rebuilt (pictured below), and the left section was reportedly demolished in 2004.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/NintendoCards.jpg/250px-NintendoCards.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NintendoCards.jpg)

Nintendo [karuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karuta "Karuta") poster from the [Meiji era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_era "Meiji era")

Nintendo was founded as Nintendo Koppai[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-10) on 23 September 1889[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_founding_date-8)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_is_founded,_September_23,_1889-11) by craftsman [Fusajiro Yamauchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusajiro_Yamauchi "Fusajiro Yamauchi") in [Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimogy%C5%8D-ku,_Kyoto "Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto"), Japan, as an unincorporated establishment, to produce and distribute [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Japan "Culture of Japan")[playing cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playing_card "Playing card"), or [karuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karuta "Karuta") (かるた; from [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language")_carta_, 'card'), most notably _[hanafuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanafuda "Hanafuda")_ ([花札](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E8%8A%B1%E6%9C%AD "wikt:花札"), 'flower cards').[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_Profile-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_Probably_Doesn't_Mean_What_You_Think_It_Does-12)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-The_Traditional_Beauty_Of_Nintendo's_Playing_Cards-13)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff199914-14) The name "Nintendo" is commonly assumed to mean "leave luck to heaven",[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff199914-14)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo's_1955_Cameo_In_The_New_York_Times-15) but the assumption lacks historical validation; it has also been suggested to mean "the temple of free _hanafuda_", but even descendants of Yamauchi do not know the true intended meaning of the name.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_Probably_Doesn't_Mean_What_You_Think_It_Does-12) Hanafuda cards had become popular after Japan banned most forms of gambling in 1882, though tolerated hanafuda. Sales of hanafuda cards were popular with the [yakuza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuza "Yakuza")-run gaming parlors in Kyoto. Other card manufacturers had opted to leave the market, not wanting to be associated with its criminality, but Yamauchi persisted despite such fears to become the primary producer of hanafuda within a few years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-The_birthplace_of_Nintendo-16) With the increase of the cards' popularity, Yamauchi hired assistants to [mass-produce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_production "Mass production") them to satisfy the demand.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Before_Mario:_Nintendo's_Playing_Cards,_Toys_And_Love_Hotels-17) Even with a favorable start, the business faced financial struggles due to operating in a [niche market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niche_market "Niche market"), the slow and expensive manufacturing process, high product price, alongside long durability of the cards, which impacted sales due to the low replacement rate.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a16-18) As a solution, Nintendo produced a cheaper and lower-quality line of playing cards, _Tengu_, while also conducting product offerings in other cities such as [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), where card game profits were high. In addition, local merchants were interested in the prospect of continuous renewal of decks, thus avoiding the suspicions that reusing cards would generate.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a17-19)

According to Nintendo, the business' first western-style card deck was put on the market in 1902,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) although other documents indicate the date was 1907, shortly after the [Russo-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a19-20) Although the cards were initially intended to be exported, they quickly gained popularity within and without Japan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) During this time, the business styled itself as Marufuku Nintendo Card Co.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo's_oldest_playing_cards?_Marufuku_No._1-21) The [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War") created considerable difficulties for companies in the leisure sector, which were subject to new levies such as the _[Karuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karuta "Karuta") Zei_ ("playing cards tax").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a20-22) Nintendo subsisted and, in 1907, entered into an agreement with Nihon Senbai—later known as the [Japan Tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Tobacco "Japan Tobacco")—to market its cards to various cigarette stores throughout the country.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a21-23) A Nintendo promotional calendar from the [Taishō era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taish%C5%8D_era "Taishō era") dated to 1915 indicates that the business was named Yamauchi Nintendo[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-24) but still used the Marufuku Nintendo Co. brand for its playing cards.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-100_year_old_Nintendo_promotional_calendar-25)

[Japanese culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Japan "Culture of Japan") stipulated that for Nintendo to continue as a family business after Yamauchi's retirement, Yamauchi had to adopt his son-in-law so that he could take over the business. As a result, [Sekiryo Kaneda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sekiryo_Kaneda "Sekiryo Kaneda") adopted the Yamauchi surname in 1907 and headed the business in 1929. By that time, Nintendo was the largest playing card business in Japan.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff199915-26)

#### 1933–1968: Incorporation and expansion

[![Image 16: 1933–1959, in Shimogyō-ku, Kyoto](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Nintendo_Former_Headquarters_Building.jpg/250px-Nintendo_Former_Headquarters_Building.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_Former_Headquarters_Building.jpg)

Former Nintendo headquarters (1933–1959), rebuilt from the right section of the original building

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Nintendo_former_headquarter_plate_Kyoto.jpg/250px-Nintendo_former_headquarter_plate_Kyoto.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_former_headquarter_plate_Kyoto.jpg)

English company information plate in the former Nintendo headquarters

In 1933, Sekiryo Kaneda established the company as a [general partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_partnership "General partnership") named Yamauchi Nintendo & Co., Ltd.[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-27)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) investing in the construction of a new corporate headquarters located next to the original building,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff2011-28) near the [Toba-kaidō train station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba-kaid%C5%8D_Station "Toba-kaidō Station").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-29) Because Sekiryo's marriage to Yamauchi's daughter produced no male heirs, he planned to adopt his son-in-law Shikanojo Inaba, an artist in the company's employ and the father of his grandson [Hiroshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshi_Yamauchi "Hiroshi Yamauchi"), born in 1927. However, Inaba abandoned his family and the company, so Hiroshi was made Sekiryo's eventual successor.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff199916-30)

[World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") negatively impacted the company as Japanese authorities prohibited the diffusion of foreign card games, and as the priorities of Japanese society shifted, its interest in recreational activities waned. During this time, Nintendo was partly supported by a financial injection from Hiroshi's wife Michiko Inaba, who came from a wealthy family.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a23-31) In 1947, Sekiryo founded the distribution company Marufuku Co., Ltd.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-32) responsible for Nintendo's sales and marketing operations, which would eventually go on to become the present-day Nintendo Co., Ltd., in Higashikawara-cho, Imagumano, [Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higashiyama-ku,_Kyoto "Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_Probably_Doesn't_Mean_What_You_Think_It_Does-12)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Nintendo_1949_New_Year_staff_commemoration.webp/500px-Nintendo_1949_New_Year_staff_commemoration.webp?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo_1949_New_Year_staff_commemoration.webp)

1949 New Year Nintendo staff commemoration

In 1950, due to Sekiryo's deteriorating health,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a24-33) Hiroshi Yamauchi assumed the presidency and headed manufacturing operations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) His first actions involved several important changes in the operation of the company: in 1951, he changed the company name to Nintendo Playing Card Co., Ltd.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-34)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Vooks-35) and in the following year, he centralized the manufacturing facilities dispersed in Kyoto, which led to the expansion of the offices in Kamitakamatsu-cho, Fukuine, Higashiyama-ku, Kyoto.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a25-36) In 1953, Nintendo became the first company to succeed in mass-producing plastic playing cards in Japan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) Some of the company's employees, accustomed to more cautious and conservative leadership, viewed the new measures with concern, and the rising tension led to a call for a [strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_action "Strike action"). However, the measure had no major impact, as Hiroshi resorted to the dismissal of several dissatisfied workers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a26-37)

In 1959, Nintendo moved its headquarters to Kamitakamatsu-cho, Fukuine, Higashiyama-ku in [Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto"). The company entered into a partnership with [Walt Disney Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Animation_Studios "Walt Disney Animation Studios") to incorporate its characters into playing cards, which opened it up to the children's market and resulted in a boost to Nintendo's playing card business.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Vooks-35) Nintendo automated the production of Japanese playing cards using backing paper, and also developed a distribution system that allowed it to offer its products in toy stores.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff2011-28) By 1961, the company had established a Tokyo branch in [Chiyoda, Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiyoda,_Tokyo "Chiyoda, Tokyo"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4) and sold more than 1.5 million card packs, holding a high [market share](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_share "Market share"), for which it relied on televised advertising campaigns.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a28-38) In 1962, Nintendo became a public company by listing stock on the second section of the [Osaka Securities Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka_Exchange "Osaka Exchange") and the Kyoto Stock Exchange.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) In the following year, the company adopted its current name, Nintendo & Co., Ltd.[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-39) and started manufacturing games in addition to playing cards.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)

In 1964, Nintendo earned ¥150 million.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a29-40) Although the company experienced a period of economic prosperity, the Disney cards and derived products made it dependent on the children's market. The situation was exacerbated by the falling sales of its adult-oriented playing cards caused by Japanese society gravitating toward other hobbies such as [pachinko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachinko "Pachinko"), [bowling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling "Bowling"), and nightly outings.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a28-38) When Disney card sales began to decline, Nintendo realized that it had no real alternative to alleviate the situation.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a29-40) After the 1964 [Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics"), Nintendo's stock price plummeted to its lowest recorded level of ¥60.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-41)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-42)

In 1965, Nintendo hired [Gunpei Yokoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpei_Yokoi "Gunpei Yokoi") to maintain the assembly-line machines used to manufacture its playing cards.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-43)

#### 1969–1972: Classic and electronic toys

Yamauchi increased Nintendo's investment in a research and development department in 1969, directed by Hiroshi Imanishi, a long-time employee of the company. Yokoi was moved to the newly created department and was responsible for coordinating various projects.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff199920%E2%80%9321-44) Yokoi's experience in manufacturing electronic devices led Yamauchi to put him in charge of the company's games department, and his products would be mass-produced.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-BusinessInsider2019-45) During that period, Nintendo built a new production plant in [Uji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uji "Uji"), just outside of Kyoto,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) and distributed classic [tabletop games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabletop_game "Tabletop game") like [chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess"), [shogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shogi "Shogi"), [go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_(game) "Go (game)"), and [mahjong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahjong "Mahjong"), and other foreign games under the Nippon Game brand.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a32-46) The company's restructuring preserved a couple of areas dedicated to playing card manufacturing.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a33-47)

In 1970, the company's stock listing was promoted to the first section of the Osaka Stock Exchange,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Corporate_Information_:_Company_History-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) and the reconstruction and enlargement of its corporate headquarters was completed.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) The year represented a watershed moment in Nintendo's history as it released Japan's first electronic toy—the _Beam Gun_, an [optoelectronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optoelectronics "Optoelectronics") pistol designed by [Masayuki Uemura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masayuki_Uemura "Masayuki Uemura").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) In total, more than a million units were sold.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff199924-48) Nintendo partnered with [Magnavox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnavox "Magnavox") to provide a [light gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_gun "Light gun") controller based on the _Beam Gun_ design for the company's new home video game console, the [Magnavox Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnavox_Odyssey "Magnavox Odyssey"), in 1971.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-49) Other popular toys released at the time included the [Ultra Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_Hand "Ultra Hand"), the [Ultra Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_Machine "Ultra Machine"), the Ultra Scope, and the [Love Tester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Tester "Love Tester"), all designed by Yokoi. More than 1.2 million units of Ultra Hand were sold in Japan.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Before_Mario:_Nintendo's_Playing_Cards,_Toys_And_Love_Hotels-17)

#### 1973–1978: Early video games and Color TV-Game

Further information: [History of Color TV-Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_TV-Game#History "Color TV-Game")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Nintendo-Color-TV-Game-Blockbreaker-FL.png/250px-Nintendo-Color-TV-Game-Blockbreaker-FL.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nintendo-Color-TV-Game-Blockbreaker-FL.png)

The [Color TV-Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_TV-Game "Color TV-Game")

The growing demand for Nintendo's products led Yamauchi to further expand the offices, for which he acquired the surrounding land and assigned the production of cards to the original Nintendo building. Meanwhile, Yokoi, Uemura, and new employees such as [Genyo Takeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genyo_Takeda "Genyo Takeda") continued to develop innovative products for the company.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff2011-28) The [Laser Clay Shooting System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_Clay_Shooting_System "Laser Clay Shooting System") was released in 1973 and managed to surpass bowling in popularity. Though Nintendo's toys continued to gain popularity, the [1973 oil crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis") caused both a spike in the cost of plastics and a change in consumer priorities that put essential products over pastimes, and Nintendo lost several billion yen.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-vice_yokoi-50)

In 1974, Nintendo released _[Wild Gunman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild\_Gunman "Wild Gunman")_, a [skeet shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeet_shooting "Skeet shooting") arcade simulation consisting of a [16 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16_mm_film "16 mm film") image projector with a sensor that detects a beam from the player's [light gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_gun "Light gun"). Both the Laser Clay Shooting System and _Wild Gunman_ were successfully exported to Europe and North America.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) However, Nintendo's production speeds were still slow compared to rival companies such as [Bandai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandai "Bandai") and [Tomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomy "Tomy"), and their prices were high, which led to the discontinuation of some of their light gun products.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a36-51) The subsidiary Nintendo Leisure System Co., Ltd., which developed these products, was closed as a result of the economic impact dealt by the oil crisis.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGorges2015a183-52)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_%28cropped_4%29.jpg/250px-Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_%28cropped_4%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_(cropped_4).jpg)

[Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto") joined Nintendo in 1977.

Yamauchi, motivated by the successes of [Atari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari "Atari") and Magnavox with their [video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console "Video game console"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-FOOTNOTESheff2011-28) acquired the Japanese distribution rights for the Magnavox Odyssey in 1974,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-BusinessInsider2019-45) and reached an agreement with [Mitsubishi Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsubishi_Electric "Mitsubishi Electric") to develop similar products between 1975 and 1978, including the first [microprocessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microprocessor "Microprocessor") for video games systems, the [Color TV-Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_TV-Game "Color TV-Game") series, and an arcade game inspired by [Othello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reversi "Reversi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-Nintendo_History-5) During this period, Takeda developed the video game _[EVR Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EVR\_Race "EVR Race")_,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-53) and [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto") joined Yokoi's team with the responsibility of designing the casing for the Color TV-Game consoles.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-54) In 1978, Nintendo's research and development department was split into two facilities, [Nintendo Research & Development 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Research_&_Development_1 "Nintendo Research & Development 1") and [Nintendo Research & Development 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Research_&_Development_2 "Nintendo Research & Development 2"), respectively managed by Yokoi and Uemura.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-55)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-56)

Shigeru Miyamoto brought distinctive sources of inspiration to the company, ranging from the [natural environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment") and regional culture of [Sonobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonobe,_Kyoto "Sonobe, Kyoto"), to popular culture influences like [Westerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_(genre) "Western (genre)") and [detective fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_detective_fiction "Japanese detective fiction"), and to folk [Shinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinto "Shinto") practices and [family media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_media "Christian media").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-57)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-58)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-59)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-60) They are seen in most of Nintendo's major franchises which developed following Miyamoto's creative leadership.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo#cite_note-The_Father_of_Modern_Video_Games-61)

#### 1979–1987: Game & Watch, arcade games, and Nintendo Entertainment System

Further information: [History of Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch#Origin_and_design "Game & Watch") and [History of Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "History of the Nintendo Entertainment System")
